title: Finite Measured Entropy Production Does Not Imply Finite Microscopic Irreversibility
authors: Hieu Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coarse-grained measurements provide a lower bound on entropy production, but how much microscopic irreversibility can they conceal? We construct a driven quantum system in which an imperfect counter registers a finite, strictly positive arrow of time while the microscopic entropy production is infinite. The system is a degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold, coupled to a thermal reservoir through repeated interactions with bosonic ancillas. The oscillator sustains a finite, positive heat current into the vacuum bath, where absorption is forbidden and forward and reverse trajectory laws have different supports. A photon counter with finite collection efficiency, gated time bins, and independent dark counts defines a common coarse-graining of the aligned trajectory laws. For fixed observation duration [MATH] and detector parameters, we prove that the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as the bath temperature [MATH] vanishes and is strictly positive at vacuum. The hidden contribution obeys [MATH], where [MATH] is the stationary vacuum heat current. False positives conceal the support mismatch while preserving measurable time asymmetry. Thus, finite and informative measurements of entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility.
tldr: The paper constructs a driven quantum system where coarse-grained measurements register finite positive entropy production while the microscopic entropy production is infinite.
motivation: Coarse-grained measurements lower-bound entropy production, but it is unclear how much microscopic irreversibility they can hide; this work probes whether finite observed arrow-of-time signals can coexist with divergent microscopic entropy production.
method: A degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold is coupled to a thermal reservoir via repeated interactions with bosonic ancillas, and a photon counter with finite efficiency, gated bins, and dark counts defines a common coarse-graining of forward and reverse trajectory laws.
result: For fixed observation duration and detector parameters, the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as bath temperature vanishes and is strictly positive at vacuum, while the hidden contribution diverges with the stationary vacuum heat current.
conclusion: Finite and informative measurements of entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility, with false positives concealing support mismatch while preserving measurable time asymmetry.

The key mechanism is that the oscillator maintains a positive heat current into the vacuum bath, where absorption is forbidden, leading to forward and reverse trajectory ensembles with disjoint supports. The counter's coarse-graining, including false positives from dark counts, creates overlapping supports that conceal the divergence while preserving measurable time asymmetry. The authors prove that for fixed observation duration and detector parameters, the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as T_b → 0 and is strictly positive at vacuum. They derive that the hidden contribution to entropy production scales as Σ_hid(𝒯,T_b) = 𝒯 Q̇_0/(k_B T_b) + O(1), with Q̇_0 > 0 the stationary vacuum heat current. title: Packet-wise Multi-hop Quantum Routing Of Hybrid Quantum-classical Packets
authors: Tae Yeong Park, Youn Chang Jeong, Myeong Soo Kang, Kwang Yong Song, Paul G. Kwiat, Hee Su Park
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13625v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The ability to dynamically route quantum information across multiple nodes is a key requirement for realizing versatile and scalable quantum networks. Quantum routers are devices to achieve packet-level routing beyond static point-to-point connections by handling hybrid packets combining classical headers and quantum payloads. Previously proposed methods have selectively accessed the classical and quantum components of the packets utilizing wavelength splitters and optical switches, and repacked the hybrid packets before transmission through the outgoing link with regenerating classical headers. This work reports a novel optical-fiber-based quantum router that minimizes the disturbance and latency on the hybrid packets through more transparent operation. We experimentally demonstrate double-hop routing via two cascaded routers to three distinct receivers without regeneration of the headers. As a practical application, quantum key distribution packets based on time-bin qubits and a BB84 protocol with a two-decoy-state method are successfully delivered to the three receivers achieving nonzero secret key rates. These results demonstrate the feasibility of extensive quantum networks interconnected by multiple-step router nodes.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a transparent fiber-based quantum router that routes hybrid quantum-classical packets over two cascaded hops to three receivers, including QKD payload delivery.
motivation: Scalable quantum networks require dynamic packet-level routing across multiple nodes rather than static point-to-point links, but previous routers disturb packets and regenerate classical headers.
method: The authors design an optical-fiber-based quantum router for hybrid packets with classical headers and quantum payloads, minimizing disturbance and latency through more transparent operation, and test double-hop routing via two cascaded routers to three receivers.
result: They successfully deliver time-bin BB84 QKD packets with two-decoy-state method to three receivers over two hops without header regeneration, achieving nonzero secret key rates.
conclusion: The results support the feasibility of extensive multi-node quantum networks interconnected by cascaded quantum router nodes.

title: Second-level Termination Of The Ppt Entanglement-cost Hierarchy For Two Qutrits
authors: Wei Song, Xiao-Lan Zong, Ming Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.12993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that for arbitrary two-qutrit quantum states, the semidefinite programming lower-bound hierarchy for the PPT entanglement cost terminates at the second level. Therefore, under operations preserving positive partial transpose, its zero-error asymptotic entanglement cost can be obtained by a semidefinite program involving only three Hermitian matrix variables. The key to the proof is to shorten the feasible dual chain by one level; to this end, we combine finite certificates verified by exact rational arithmetic with analytic estimates near the boundary of the parameter domain. This result shows that a unified terminating level exists for two-qutrit systems, whereas no unified terminating level exists for all dimensions.
tldr: The paper proves that the semidefinite-programming lower-bound hierarchy for the PPT entanglement cost of arbitrary two-qutrit states terminates at the second level.
motivation: PPT entanglement cost is a key operational entanglement measure under PPT-preserving operations, but its computability generally relies on infinite SDP hierarchies; determining when these hierarchies terminate is important for practical and theoretical entanglement quantification.
method: The authors shorten the feasible dual chain by one level, combining exact rational-arithmetic finite certificates with analytic estimates near the boundary of the parameter domain.
result: For all two-qutrit states, the zero-error asymptotic entanglement cost under PPT-preserving operations is computable via an SDP with only three Hermitian matrix variables, and a unified terminating level exists for two qutrits, unlike in general dimensions.
conclusion: This establishes a dimension-specific termination result for the PPT entanglement-cost hierarchy and provides a finite SDP characterization for two-qutrit systems.

title: Time Direction Entanglement Entropy Of Free Fermion Ground States
authors: Xinyu Sun, Bowei Liu, Joshua Yi, Biao Lian
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While the entanglement entropy of a spatial subregion has been extensively studied, a properly defined entanglement entropy of quantum states in a time direction interval remains underexplored. We investigate the scaling behaviors of the recently defined time direction entanglement entropy (TDEE) for free fermion quantum states, which is computed from the reduced density matrix of a sub-Hilbert space that minimally supports all the time-evolved operators in the time direction interval. Based on the Fisher--Hartwig conjecture for Toeplitz matrices, we develop an analytical framework for understanding the TDEE in a time interval with discrete time step [MATH]. For disorderless one-dimensional (1D) systems (gapless fermions or band insulators), in different regimes of gap, bandwidth and [MATH], we find the TDEE can exhibit area law (for nonzero gap), logarithmic law or volume law in the length of time. For 1D Anderson insulators, we numerically find the TDEE shows a Page-curve like behavior, growing at short time, and decaying in power-law at long time exceeding the crossover time determined by localization. In the continuum time limit [MATH], the TDEE of disorderless gapless fermions, band insulators and Anderson insulators exhibit logarithmic law, area law and sub-area law, respectively. We also show that the sub-Hilbert space of a time-direction interval stabilizes in the [MATH] limit, which is understandable as a subspace of the Hilbert space of the Lieb-Robinson causal diamond.
tldr: The paper analytically and numerically studies a recently defined time-direction entanglement entropy for free-fermion states, deriving area-, logarithmic-, volume-law, and Page-curve-like scaling behaviors across gapless, gapped, and disordered regimes.
motivation: Spatial entanglement entropy is well studied, but entanglement entropy associated with a time interval remains underexplored, motivating a systematic characterization of time-direction entanglement in free-fermion systems.
method: The authors define TDEE via the reduced density matrix of the minimal sub-Hilbert space supporting time-evolved operators in a discrete time interval and analyze Toeplitz matrix asymptotics using the Fisher-Hartwig conjecture, complemented by numerical studies of Anderson insulators.
result: For disorderless 1D systems, TDEE exhibits area-law, logarithmic, or volume-law scaling depending on gap, bandwidth, and time step; for 1D Anderson insulators it shows Page-curve-like growth followed by power-law decay, with continuum limits giving logarithmic, area, and sub-area laws for gapless, band-insulator, and Anderson-insulator cases respectively.
conclusion: Time-direction entanglement entropy provides a distinct diagnostic of quantum state structure and dynamics, with scaling laws tied to spectral gaps, disorder localization, and causal-diamond Hilbert-space structure.

TDEE is defined as the entanglement entropy of a reduced density matrix associated with a sub-Hilbert space that minimally supports all time-evolved operators within a time interval of length T, discretized into steps τ. The authors develop an analytical framework based on the Fisher-Hartwig conjecture for Toeplitz matrices to compute TDEE for one-dimensional (1D) free fermion systems, including gapless fermions, band insulators, and Anderson insulators. They consider both disorderless and disordered cases, and examine the dependence on the gap, bandwidth, and time step τ. Key findings include: for disorderless 1D systems, TDEE exhibits area law (for nonzero gap), logarithmic law, or volume law in the time length depending on the regime; for 1D Anderson insulators, TDEE shows a Page-curve-like behavior, growing at short times and decaying as a power law at long times, with a crossover time determined by localization length. The authors also show that the sub-Hilbert space stabilizes in the τ→0 limit, interpretable as a subspace of the Lieb-Robinson causal diamond.

title: Quantized Memory Of Measurement Records Near The Light Cone Of Quantum Circuits
authors: Jamal Slim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13175v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processors now measure qubits in the middle of a circuit, and the stream of outcomes is the raw output of error correction, measurement-based state preparation and monitored dynamics. For a scrambling circuit, predicting the statistics of this stream is as hard as simulating the processor, so there is no exact reference to check it against once the device outgrows classical simulation. We show that near the light cone the problem becomes exactly solvable, for any two-qubit gate. In a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, measurements along the edge of the light cone form a two-state Markov chain, and measurements [MATH] sites inside the edge are generated by [MATH] qubits that move with it, while the rest of the chain, however large, acts on them as a memoryless bath. The memory of the record is therefore quantized, one bit on the edge and at most one more for every site of displacement, a bound that generic gates attain. The same causal structure determines which hardware noise the record can see, removes that sensitivity at no gate cost, and yields a tomography-free witness of dual-unitarity. On a 156-qubit superconducting processor, a demonstration with its analysis specified in advance finds the predicted memory one and two sites inside the light cone, and none where the theory forbids it. This gives dynamic circuits an exact reference at any system size, and shows that the collision models of open-system theory arise exactly inside chaotic dynamics.
tldr: Shows that measurement records near the light cone of scrambling brickwork circuits have quantized memory and form an exactly solvable Markov process, verified on a 156-qubit superconducting processor.
motivation: Mid-circuit measurement records are central to error correction, measurement-based state preparation, and monitored dynamics, but their statistics are generally hard to predict once a scrambling device exceeds classical simulation.
method: The paper analytically studies record statistics near the light cone for any two-qubit gate in a brickwork circuit with one polarized qubit in a maximally mixed background, then tests the predictions on a 156-qubit superconducting processor.
result: Measurements along the light-cone edge form a two-state Markov chain, with one bit of memory on the edge and at most one additional bit per site of displacement; the experiment confirms the predicted memory inside the light cone and none where forbidden.
conclusion: The work provides an exact, tomography-free reference for dynamic-circuit measurement statistics at arbitrary system size and shows that collision models of open-system theory arise inside chaotic quantum dynamics.

title: Third-Order Quantum Information From Distributed Randomized Measurements
authors: Giovanni Scala, Corrado Cosimo Mattiacci, Gniewomir Sarbicki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized measurements offer a way to probe nonlinear properties of quantum states without reconstructing their full density matrices. For states shared between distant laboratories, we study products of three outcome probabilities measured at the same local settings and then averaged over independent local random unitaries. We determine, for an arbitrary number of parties, which third-order local-unitary invariant combinations these averages retain and which they cannot separate. The accessible information is encoded in algebraic invariants of the quantum state and is reconstructed by analysing the permutation symmetries induced by the distributed measurement protocol. Exploiting these symmetries, the reconstruction problem collapses, regardless of the number of measurement outcomes, to the symbolic inversion of a 3 x 3 matrix. As a result, nonlinear information can be extracted without inverting the exponentially large matrices that typically arise in distributed multipartite quantum systems.

method: The authors average products of three outcome probabilities at the same local settings over independent local random unitaries and analyze the permutation symmetries induced by the distributed protocol.
result: They determine the accessible third-order local-unitary invariant combinations for an arbitrary number of parties and show that reconstruction collapses, independent of measurement-outcome count, to symbolic inversion of a 3x3 matrix.
conclusion: The protocol provides an efficient way to extract nonlinear quantum information in distributed multipartite systems without exponential matrix inversion, with the accessible information encoded in algebraic invariants of the state.

title: How Wide Must An Eavesdropper Be? Leakage Of A Toric-code Logical Bit To A Strip And The Nishimori Point
authors: Konstantinos Karagiannis
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.

motivation: Fault-tolerant architectures split logical qubits across decoder modules and shared readout lines, raising the question of how much a bounded region of the code actually leaks about a logical bit.
method: The authors derive an exact identity relating an observer's optimal guessing advantage to the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding restricted to a region, then analyze strip geometries via a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix (width up to 16) and emulate strip adversaries on IBM Heron d=3,5 processors.
result: A region missing a single column learns nothing, while spanning regions are protected only at impractical distances; under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip leaks as little as one row, yet below threshold the required eavesdropper width grows only as ln d, and the strip's operational threshold coincides with the Nishimori point, located to within a few thousandths.
conclusion: Geometry rather than noise governs protection, width is a poor proxy for risk, and the results yield concrete design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout, with hardware data confirming a predicted jump at width three.

title: Machine-learning Decoders For Fusion-based Quantum Computing In Real Time
authors: Daniel Barter, Jacob C. Bridgeman, Chris Dawson, Terry Farrelly, Shane Fleming, Mercedes Gimeno-Segovia, Paul Hartke, Timothy Hein, Sean Howell, Gregory Hyegang Jun, Siddhartha Kamalakara, Yehua Liu, Jose M. Monsalve Diaz, Eddie Richter, Sam Roberts
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.
tldr: PRISM is a transformer-based machine-learning decoder for fusion-based photonic quantum computing that exploits known erasure locations and achieves integer-programming-level accuracy with real-time FPGA latency.
motivation: Fault-tolerant photonic quantum computing requires decoders that handle high erasure rates from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements while meeting stringent latency, throughput, and scalability constraints.
method: The authors introduce a transformer-based decoder trained for surface, color, and quantum LDPC codes under Pauli and erasure errors, then optimize its implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA for real-time operation.
result: PRISM matches integer-programming decoders' logical error rates across distances up to 24 and error rates up to 50% of threshold, while decoding distance-8 logical blocks in both space and time with 6.59 microseconds latency and 1.56 microseconds amortized time.
conclusion: Machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures, supporting practical real-time QEC in photonic fusion-based systems.

title: Long-range Correlated Quantum Errors From Diffuson-correlated Dephasing
authors: M. E. Flatt\'e N. R. S. van Venrooij
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrical solid-state qubits are generally initialized, manipulated and read out through diffusive conductors. We show that the disorder-induced low energy modes of such a conductor --- diffusons --- impose spatially correlated dephasing on any qubits that share it, a mechanism we term diffuson-correlated dephasing. Starting from a Keldysh nonlinear sigma model for the disordered conductive region, coupled capacitively to two-level systems, we obtain the noise kernel in closed form. It decays as the inverse square of the qubit separation and changes sign with the orientation of the pair, so that qubit pairs at equal separation may be correlated or anticorrelated, an unambiguous experimental signature. In two dimensions, the correlated noise a single qubit shares with the rest of the array, in the worst-case scenario, grows logarithmically with array size rather than converging. The sufficient condition for fault tolerance under correlated noise is therefore violated, so standard threshold theorems no longer guarantee protection against this channel for large qubit arrays. As this dephasing originates from the soft-mode content of the environment rather than on any specific gate detail, we expect correlated dephasing channels of this kind wherever solid-state qubits or sensors share a gapless conductive medium.

result: The noise decays as inverse-square separation, changes sign with pair orientation, and in two dimensions the worst-case correlated noise per qubit grows logarithmically with array size, violating a sufficient condition for fault tolerance.
conclusion: Diffuson-correlated dephasing is a generic correlated-error channel for solid-state qubits sharing a gapless conductive medium, so standard threshold guarantees may not protect large qubit arrays.

title: Syndrome Extraction For Quantum Ldpc Codes In Silicon: Distributed Entanglement And Mobile Ancillas
authors: Jonathan Baugh William Chow
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can reduce the number of data qubits required per logical qubit, but their checks require long-range interactions on a planar device. We develop a singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network. Spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, where local operations consume them to measure non-local stabilizers. We construct two syndrome-extraction circuits, based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, and evaluate them using hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations. We compare these circuits with CAbLECAR, which transports a mobile ancilla between the data qubits of each check. Teleportation can outperform CAbLECAR on its original layout when transport includes spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on our node lattice, however, shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 [MATH]m and lowers its logical error rate up to 50-fold in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport then achieves a lower logical error rate than either singlet circuit at every sampled Gross-code point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below about [MATH]-[MATH], roughly half the value assumed here. Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order reveals a trade-off between shorter routes and the correlated errors produced by ancilla faults. Source heralding improves both singlet circuits, whereas phase purification helps the GHZ circuit only above a noise-dependent crossover and worsens teleportation throughout. These results show that the physical layout and interaction order can be as consequential as the choice of extraction circuit, and that cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily produce a more reliable logical memory.

title: FusionQ: A Generic And Optimal Decoding Framework For Ultra-Low-Latency Quantum Error Correction
authors: Junyu Zhou, Sean Garner, Aarthi Sundaram, Gushu Li, Yue Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) decoding has traditionally been organized around fixed decoding instances: a monolithic space-time detector error model (DEM), or a predetermined temporal window, is handed to a backend decoder after enough syndrome data has arrived. This paper presents FusionQ, a fusion decoding framework that changes this paradigm by deriving local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome and then fusing their results into a single global correction. Instead of forcing every shot through the same global or windowed problem, FusionQ builds open-boundary local DEMs around fired detector clusters and expands the corresponding footprints only when a local optimum uses virtual boundary errors. FusionQ is generic in the decoder backend: the scheduler requires only a local solution and a boundary-use flag, so exact solvers, matching-style decoders on graphlike DEMs, and heuristic decoders can share the same runtime. We prove a compositional optimality theorem: with an exact minimum-weight local backend and boundary-free publication, fusing the published local decoding results yields a global most-likely error (MLE) solution of the original DEM. Our evaluation shows that, with an exact backend, FusionQ matches the monolithic MLE result on every shot. Across decoder backends, FusionQ substantially reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition.

motivation: Traditional QEC decoding treats each shot as a monolithic or fixed-window decoding problem, which limits latency and flexibility across decoder backends. The paper aims to exploit locality in the syndrome to overlap decoding with syndrome acquisition.

result: The authors prove a compositional optimality theorem showing that exact local minimum-weight decoding with boundary-free publication yields a global most-likely-error solution, and experiments show matching MLE results with an exact backend plus substantial latency reduction across backends.
conclusion: FusionQ provides a generic and theoretically grounded decoding architecture that can reduce QEC decoding latency while preserving optimality under exact local decoding assumptions.

Specifically, the method identifies a small subset of priors to perturb—those that are likely to be unreliable due to quantum degeneracy or short cycles—and adjusts their LLRs by offsets that reflect the discrepancy between the current posterior beliefs and the messages being passed. The message-passing rules themselves remain unchanged, so the approach is compatible with any BP variant. The authors evaluate PriorTilt using circuit-level noise simulations on three quantum LDPC codes: a [[144,12,12]] Gross code (BB144), and two other benchmark codes (likely surface codes or other quantum LDPC codes). They compare against Relay-BP, a state-of-the-art BP decoder that uses relayed messages, and a beam search decoder. The decoding performance is measured in terms of logical error rate and mean decoding time. The perturbation fraction is kept very low (less than 0.5% per round on average), ensuring minimal computational overhead.

title: Frustration-free Control For Quantum-state Preparation: An Exact First-passage Theory
authors: T. D\"orstel, T. C. Lang, T. Iadecola, J. H. Wilson, M. Buchhold
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum circuits based on local measurements and feedback can autonomously prepare and stabilize entangled many-body states. In frustration-free control, the target manifold is specified by local constraints, whose violations are detected by measurement and removed by feedback. We develop an exact theory of this mechanism for the preparation of Dicke states of [MATH] qubits. Dicke states span the permutation-symmetric subspace, one per magnetization sector. Local singlet projectors define the constraints and detect departures from permutation symmetry. The resulting dynamics closes exactly on the span of the [MATH] singlet-pair projectors and is equivalent to a classical first-passage process: measurements move the pair endpoints, while feedback absorbs pairs on measured bonds. The closure reduces the exponentially large many-body Liouvillian to a generator of polynomial size. In one dimension we solve this process in closed form. Its slowest rate, [MATH] in units of the measurement rate, is an exact Liouvillian eigenvalue. For any scheme of this class, the relaxation time is bounded below by the inverse fraction of pair configurations on which feedback acts; local feedback reaches [MATH] of [MATH] configurations, requiring a time at least linear in [MATH]. A second exact closure determines the final state reached from any initial condition. Extensions to modified transport, restricted feedback, and physical errors yield an exact transport-to-absorber crossover, geometric preparation laws, and a bound on the stationary leakage. An exact second-moment closure determines the ensemble fluctuations: the measurement noise is conserving, while feedback generates removal shot noise and pair correlations. Preparation, acceleration, robustness, and fluctuations are thus governed by one exactly solvable process: the transport and absorption of local constraint violations.

method: Local singlet projectors define constraints whose violations are detected by measurements and removed by feedback; the dynamics closes exactly onto singlet-pair configurations and maps to a classical first-passage process, reducing the many-body Liouvillian to polynomial size.
result: In one dimension the process is solved in closed form, yielding exact Liouvillian eigenvalues, relaxation-time lower bounds, the final state from arbitrary initial conditions, and exact fluctuation statistics from a second-moment closure.
conclusion: Frustration-free control of Dicke-state preparation is governed by one exactly solvable transport-and-absorption process, enabling quantitative design, acceleration, and robustness analysis.

title: Time Running Backwards, And Where It Stops: Superoscillations Of Proper Time And The Memory Of The Environment
authors: Avshalom C. Elitzur Yakir Aharonov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.12971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum system prepared in a superposition of proper times - a clock whose worldline is superposed, or a clock at rest in a superposed gravitational potential - evolves, in each branch, by the same dynamics for a different duration. Post-selecting the control that sets the proper time turns the superposition into a superoscillation of the time-dilation factor: the system is found to have evolved for a proper time [MATH], where the weak value [MATH] may exceed unity, vanish, or be negative - the quantum time-translation machine of Aharonov, Anandan, Popescu and Vaidman. We ask how far back such a machine can run an irreversible process. The test system is a sealed cell - excited atoms, the radiation field they emit into, and the absorbing walls, carried as one quantum object - and the witness is projective: atoms that had begun to decay before the run are found, in the post-selected sub-ensemble, more excited than when inserted. The answer is exact and depends only on the atoms' survival amplitude. With two branches the witness holds only while the decay is younger than the memory time of the environment, after which the emission becomes Markovian. Beyond it, the post-selection amplifies the minute difference between the contents of the cell in the two branches, set by the full energy spread of the atoms and their field rather than by the linewidth, and the witness fails. Reversing a decay past the memory time requires many branches, an environment with a strictly bounded spectrum, and a post-selection probability that falls exponentially with the number of environmental oscillations to be undone. The obstacle to reversal is therefore not entropy but bandwidth - the same bandwidth that makes the emission irreversible in the first place. We give four ways to superpose a clock rate, from hollow massive shells to inertial velocities.
tldr: The paper analyzes how far a quantum time-translation machine based on superposed proper times can reverse an irreversible atomic decay, showing that the limit is set by environmental memory and bandwidth rather than entropy.
motivation: It asks whether post-selection and weak-value superoscillations can run an irreversible process backwards, and what physical resource ultimately prevents full reversal.
method: A sealed cell of excited atoms, radiation field, and absorbing walls is treated as one quantum object; post-selecting a superposed proper-time control produces a projective witness for apparent reversal of decay, quantified via the atomic survival amplitude and environmental memory time.
result: With two branches, the reversal witness works only while the decay is younger than the environment memory time; beyond that, many branches and a bounded environmental spectrum are required, with post-selection probability decaying exponentially.
conclusion: The obstacle to reversing decay is bandwidth rather than entropy, linking irreversibility to the same spectral bandwidth that makes emission Markovian and irreversible in the first place.

title: Dynamics Of R\'enyi Entanglement Entropies And Eigenstate Thermalization
authors: Pasquale Calabrese Riccardo Senese
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How is entanglement dynamics encoded in the eigenstates of the time-evolution operator? We address this question by focusing on R\'enyi entropy dynamics in deterministic chaotic Floquet models in arbitrary dimensions. Inspired by the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), we employ spectral representations of reduced density matrix moments (purity and its higher-order generalizations) whose decay through spectral dephasing captures nonequilibrium entanglement growth. These representations closely resemble those governing local-observable dynamics, but involve eigenstates in a replicated Hilbert space and observables are replaced by subsystem permutation operators, such as the swap operator for R\'enyi-2. Focusing on R\'enyi-2, we combine exact random matrix theory calculations, established ETH results and numerical tests in 1D to formulate ETH-like ans\"atze for subsystem swap matrix elements in the replicated eigenbasis and their cross-correlations with initial-state overlap statistics. In the thermodynamic limit, purity dynamics is entirely determined by smooth slowly varying functions that emerge from such statistics, paralleling generalized ETH formulations in a single replica. In the limit of large subsystems, these functions exhibit a striking structural simplification: locality of the dynamics together with bulk spectral dephasing reduce their functional dependence to a single fundamental frequency. Our formalism provides a setting where ETH-like statements naturally coexist for both arbitrarily small and large subsystem sizes. We discuss extensions of our results to higher R\'enyi entropies. Beyond clarifying the spectral foundations of entanglement dynamics, these results lay some of the groundwork for future applications of spectral filter methods to the computation of R\'enyi evolution in deterministic systems.

motivation: Entanglement growth in chaotic systems is usually studied via random circuits or hydrodynamic approaches; the authors ask how this dynamics is encoded in the eigenstates of the time-evolution operator, in analogy with the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis for local observables.
method: Using spectral representations of reduced density matrix moments in a replicated Hilbert space, they formulate ETH-style ansätze for subsystem permutation (e.g. swap) matrix elements and their cross-correlations with initial-state overlaps, combining exact random matrix theory calculations, established ETH results, and numerical tests in 1D.
result: In the thermodynamic limit purity dynamics is governed by smooth slowly varying functions analogous to generalized ETH; for large subsystems locality and bulk spectral dephasing collapse their functional dependence onto a single fundamental frequency, and extensions to higher Rényi entropies are discussed.
conclusion: The work clarifies the spectral foundations of entanglement dynamics and provides a setting where ETH-like statements hold for both small and large subsystems, laying groundwork for spectral filter methods to compute Rényi evolution in deterministic systems.

title: Classical Tensor Codes And Quantum Tanner Codes Achieve Capacity On Erasure Channels
authors: Henry D. Pfister, Oscar Sprumont, Gilles Z\'emor
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that on the classical erasure channel, the tensor product of two capacity-achieving code families is itself capacity-achieving under mild conditions. We also prove that duals of tensor products of independent uniform random binary linear codes achieve erasure capacity. Using these local codes, for every erasure probability [MATH] and every rate gap [MATH], we obtain a family of binary quantum Tanner codes of rate at least [MATH]. For fixed [MATH] and [MATH], these codes have bounded check weights, minimum distance growing linearly with the blocklength, and a linear-time erasure decoder whose decoding error decays exponentially with the blocklength.
tldr: The paper constructs classical tensor-product codes and quantum Tanner codes that achieve capacity on erasure channels with linear-time decoding and linearly growing distance.
motivation: Erasure channels provide a clean setting for understanding capacity-achieving classical and quantum error-correcting codes, with implications for reliable quantum information storage and communication.
method: The authors prove that tensor products of capacity-achieving classical code families remain capacity-achieving under mild conditions, and use random binary linear codes and their duals as local codes to build quantum Tanner codes.
result: For every erasure probability and rate gap, they obtain binary quantum Tanner codes with bounded check weights, linear minimum distance, and a linear-time erasure decoder whose error decays exponentially in blocklength.

It first establishes two classical coding results: (1) on the classical erasure channel, the tensor product of two capacity-achieving code families is itself capacity-achieving under mild conditions, and (2) the duals of tensor products of independent uniform random binary linear codes achieve erasure capacity. title: Which Data Samples Matter When Training A Quantum Model?
authors: M. Emre Sahin, Cenk T\"uys\"uz, David Galvin, Oscar Wallis, Alex Gregory, Paul Edwards, Christa Zoufal
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The expressivity, loss landscapes, and generalization behavior of quantum machine learning models have been studied extensively, yet mainly from a model-centric point of view. Little is known about the compatibility of particular quantum models with specific datasets. In this work, we study quantum machine learning models with a data-dependent focus by establishing a quantum-compatible form of the V-usable information. This metric quantifies the information a model can extract from a dataset, enabling a direct, data-centric comparison of different models. We employ this metric to study which data points contribute most significantly to a model's learning process. This enables us to develop an informed preselection strategy for data subsets that can significantly improve the data efficiency of the training pipeline. This work establishes the V-usable information as a powerful diagnostic tool for learning dynamics and a practical route to data-efficient quantum machine learning.

result: The metric enables direct data-centric model comparison and supports an informed preselection strategy that can significantly improve data efficiency in quantum model training.
conclusion: V-usable information serves as a diagnostic tool for learning dynamics and a practical route toward more data-efficient quantum machine learning.

title: A Compiler For Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
authors: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Seyong Lee, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.
tldr: The paper presents an MLIR-based compiler infrastructure for fault-tolerant quantum computing that preserves code-specific syndrome, magic-state, and Pauli-frame information through lowering to OpenQASM 3, QIR, Stim, and hardware.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires compiler intermediate representations that retain error-correcting-code choices, syndrome data, and non-Clifford resource requirements across analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering.
method: The authors develop FTQC, an open-source MLIR dialect with typed SSA values for logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames, plus an error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering, and IR-resident resource analysis.
result: Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata supports verifiable and retargetable code-specific decisions; on the 20-qubit Pathfinder, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times, and a QFT-3 magic-state factory required five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit.
conclusion: The work provides a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

title: Real-time Spectral Combs From Delayed Quantum Feedback In Multimode Cavity Qed
authors: Diego Aranda-Lozano, H\'ector M. Castro-Beltr\'an, Jos\'e R\'ecamier, Ricardo Rom\'an-Ancheyta, Carlos A. Gonz\'alez-Guti\'errez
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the time-dependent physical spectrum of light for a two-level atom coupled to a large, but discrete, number of modes of an electromagnetic cavity. Radiation emitted by the atom, placed at the center of the cavity, returns after the round-trip time [MATH], re-excites it, and is re-emitted, producing a sequence of atomic population revivals. For a coupling approximately flat over the atomic linewidth, the emission dynamics reduces to a delay-differential equation of Bixon--Jortner type. Using its analytical solution in terms of Laguerre polynomials, we investigate how successive emission and reabsorption cycles shape the time-dependent spectrum. The physical spectrum exhibits revivals during which a transient frequency comb of spacing [MATH] develops. The comb results from the quantum interference between successive emission stages; its teeth sit not at the cavity modes but at the resonances of the effective two half-cavities created by the resonantly reflecting atom. The visibility scales as [MATH] with the filter bandwidth [MATH], and at long times the comb converges to the dressed-mode spectrum, which we also obtain analytically in quantitative agreement with exact diagonalization. We show that the physical spectrum resolves the feedback phase, to which the atomic population is insensitive in the regime of well-separated emission stages, and provides additional frequency-resolved signatures of the atomic position. We discuss two feasible experimental implementations of our results with transmons (artificial atoms) coupled to microwave and surface-acoustic-wave resonators.
tldr: The authors compute the time-dependent physical spectrum of a two-level atom coupled to a discrete multimode cavity, showing that delayed quantum feedback from round-trip re-excitation generates transient spectral frequency combs whose teeth sit at effective half-cavity resonances.
motivation: Delayed coherent feedback in cavity QED is known to produce atomic population revivals, but how such feedback imprints on the frequency-resolved (physical) spectrum of emitted light, and whether that spectrum carries information invisible to population dynamics, was not established.
method: For a coupling flat over the atomic linewidth the dynamics reduces to a Bixon-Jortner-type delay-differential equation, solved analytically via Laguerre polynomials; the physical spectrum is then evaluated with a finite-bandwidth spectral filter and compared against exact diagonalization and the long-time dressed-mode spectrum.
result: The spectrum exhibits revivals forming a transient frequency comb with spacing set by the feedback round-trip time, with teeth at resonances of the two effective half-cavities defined by the reflecting atom rather than at the bare cavity modes; visibility scales as a power of the filter bandwidth, and the long-time limit converges to the analytically obtained dressed-mode spectrum in quantitative agreement with exact diagonalization.
conclusion: The physical spectrum resolves the feedback phase and the atomic position, quantities to which the atomic population is insensitive in the well-separated emission-stage regime, and the effect is proposed for implementation with transmons coupled to microwave and surface-acoustic-wave resonators.

title: Euclidean And Hermitian Self-Orthogonal Codes From Divisible Codes
authors: Chenkun Xie Ziling Heng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-orthogonality and divisibility are two fundamental properties of linear codes, and the relationship between them has long been of interest. Huffman and Pless (2003) showed that every binary \(4\)-divisible code is Euclidean self-orthogonal, that a ternary code is Euclidean self-orthogonal if and only if it is \(3\)-divisible, and that a quaternary code is Hermitian self-orthogonal if and only if it is \(2\)-divisible. The general case remained open for a long time. In 2024, Li and Heng settled the odd-characteristic case, proving that every \(p\)-divisible code over \(\F_{p^m}\), with \(p\) odd, that contains the all-one vector is Euclidean self-orthogonal. In this paper we treat the even-characteristic case: we prove that every \(4\)-divisible code over \(\F_{2^m}\) containing the all-one vector is Euclidean self-orthogonal. We also prove that, for every prime \(p\), every \(p\)-divisible linear code over \(\F_{q^2}\), where \(q=p^m\), that contains the all-one vector is Hermitian self-orthogonal. These criteria make the construction of self-orthogonal codes from divisible codes simple and efficient. As applications, we recover the known Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonality of generalized Reed--Muller codes and obtain several infinite families of new Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonal codes, which give rise to infinite families of quantum codes with excellent parameters.
tldr: The paper proves new criteria relating divisibility of linear codes over finite fields to Euclidean or Hermitian self-orthogonality, and uses them to construct quantum codes.
motivation: Self-orthogonal codes are central to constructing stabilizer/CSS quantum codes, and the relationship between divisibility and self-orthogonality has been a long-standing coding-theory question with direct relevance to quantum error correction.
method: The authors extend prior results to even characteristic, proving that every 4-divisible code over F_{2^m} containing the all-one vector is Euclidean self-orthogonal, and that for every prime p, p-divisible codes over F_{q^2} containing the all-one vector are Hermitian self-orthogonal.
result: These criteria simplify the construction of self-orthogonal codes from divisible codes; applications recover known self-orthogonality of generalized Reed-Muller codes and yield infinite families of new Euclidean and Hermitian self-orthogonal codes.
conclusion: The resulting self-orthogonal codes produce infinite families of quantum codes with excellent parameters, strengthening the bridge between divisible classical codes and quantum code construction.

title: Field-induced Phase-matching In Josephson Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifiers
authors: Daniil E. Bazulin, Simon Gandorfer, Niklas Bruckmoser, Kedar E. Honasoge, Leon Koch, Maria-Teresa Handschuh, Matthias Hirschbichler, Kirill Shulga, Achim Marx, Michael Haider, Stefan Filipp, Kirill G. Fedorov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) enable broadband, quantum-limited amplification of weak microwave signals. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a phase-matching approach using a homogeneous nonlinear medium based on Josephson elements by exploiting a magnetic field inhomogeneity. We show how the latter may lead to the sign reversal of the 3-wave mixing nonlinearity and stabilization of the parametric amplification. We envision this technique as a viable alternative to conventional phase-matching approaches.

title: Exceptional Points In non-Markovian Quantum-state Diffusion: From Coefficient Dynamics To State Signatures
authors: Yusui Chen, Hang Liu, Kaiqi Xiong, Quanzhen Ding, Eric Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An exceptional point of a memory-coefficient equation need not have the same signature in every quantum-state observable. We examine this relation within exact non-Markovian quantum-state diffusion (NMQSD), following the same operator closure from its coefficient dynamics to the non-Markovian master equation obtained by noise averaging. A finite homogeneous lift identifies the Jordan chains reached by the causal initialization, while state reconstruction determines which contributions survive in a specified readout. Two models expose the distinction. For common-bath qubits restricted to zero and one excitation, a noise-independent lowering-form [MATH] operator gives a closed master equation. Every defective decaying mode transfers its full pole order to a suitable unconditional excitation--reference coherence. A known third-order configuration illustrates both a quadratic--exponential coherence and cancellation of its highest-order term in another quadrature. For a position-coupled oscillator in a fixed-photon-number optomechanical sector, the exact closure contains a scalar noise-history term. On the regular normalizable branch studied for bath decay rates below the oscillator frequency, two second-order coefficient blocks lead to a double pole in the conditional displacement response to the NMQSD noise history, at long preparation age and fixed lag. The purely algebraic coefficient tail cancels from the conditional Gaussian width. Complete noise averaging changes the master-equation coefficients and combines conditional width with the weighted spread of state centers. Together, the models show how causal preparation, state reconstruction, and averaging give coefficient exceptional points a precise, readout-dependent meaning.

conclusion: Coefficient exceptional points acquire precise physical meaning only after accounting for causal preparation, state reconstruction, and complete noise averaging, which can modify master-equation coefficients and observable signatures.
