conclusion: The model provides a clean, exactly solvable example of a symmetry-breaking transition driven by a border-collision bifurcation in a piecewise-smooth system, with potential interpretation as a stylized competition/allocation dynamics.

title: Local Periodic Orbit Penetration In Dynamical Systems
authors: Diyath Nelaka Pannipitiya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce two complementary frameworks for studying local periodicity and recurrence in dynamical systems. In the topological setting, we consider continuous maps with nonempty periodic-point sets, restricted to the closures of their periodic points. We define the periodic penetration time of an open set as the least period of a periodic point it contains. Using dynamically refined finite generating covers, we construct asymptotic mean and variance invariants that describe local periodic penetration relative to the logarithms of minimum subcover cardinalities. We establish their invariance under topological conjugacy and investigate their behavior for finite periodic systems, full shifts, shifts of finite type, and zero-entropy systems with dense periodic points. We also extend the construction to invertible systems using symmetric dynamical refinements. In the measure theoretic setting, we define local return times through positive measure intersections of measurable sets with their iterated preimages. Using dynamically refined finite generating partitions, we construct corresponding asymptotic mean and variance invariants and establish their invariance under measure-theoretic isomorphism. We derive explicit formulas for finite probability-preserving systems and study finite periodic approximations of uniform Bernoulli shifts on [MATH] symbols, proving that their system-level mean and variance invariants converge to [MATH] and [MATH], respectively. Our results demonstrate that local periodic penetration and return-time statistics provide information about dynamical systems beyond that captured by classical entropy.
tldr: The paper introduces new asymptotic mean and variance invariants characterizing local periodic orbit penetration and return-time statistics in topological and measure-theoretic dynamical systems.
motivation: The authors aim to capture local periodicity and recurrence structure of dynamical systems in a way that goes beyond what classical entropy measures can distinguish.
method: Using dynamically refined finite generating covers (and partitions, with a symmetric extension for invertible maps), they define periodic penetration times and local return times and build asymptotic mean/variance invariants proven invariant under topological conjugacy and measure-theoretic isomorphism.
result: They compute explicit formulas for finite periodic systems and uniform Bernoulli shift approximations, showing the system-level invariants converge to specific limiting values and distinguish systems with identical entropy.
conclusion: Local periodic penetration and return-time statistics provide finer dynamical invariants than entropy alone, though the framework remains purely classical ergodic/topological dynamics.

title: Minimum Synthesis Time For Single-Deletion Correcting Codes Of Prescribed Size
authors: Yuling Li, Wenjun Yu, Gennian Ge
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DNA is a promising medium for data storage, but the high cost of DNA synthesis remains a major obstacle to its widespread deployment. In the reference-based synthesis model, synthesis time is measured by the length of the reference sequence. Previous studies have analyzed code sizes under synthesis-time constraints and constructed cost-constrained codes, including codes that correct deletions. In this paper, we study the minimum synthesis time for codes of prescribed size, considering both unrestricted codes and single-deletion correcting codes. We establish finite-length lower bounds valid for arbitrary reference sequences and upper bounds using existing [MATH]-ary differential VT codes. For fixed [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], we determine the minimum synthesis time up to an [MATH] term when the code size is [MATH]. The corresponding redundancy is [MATH] bits. In particular, for these code sizes, the minimum synthesis time for single-deletion correcting codes exceeds that for unrestricted codes by a term proportional to [MATH], and we determine its coefficient. We also derive upper and lower bounds for code sizes [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH]. These sizes correspond to redundancy [MATH] bits. For code sizes [MATH] with fixed constant [MATH], the redundancy is [MATH] bits. We give conditions under which single-deletion correcting codes exist or do not exist for all sufficiently large [MATH], together with bounds on the minimum synthesis time. These results show how code size and the single-deletion correcting constraint affect synthesis time and provide theoretical guidance for the construction of cost-constrained codes.
tldr: This paper studies the minimum synthesis time for prescribed-size single-deletion correcting codes in a reference-based DNA data storage model.
motivation: DNA synthesis cost and time are major barriers to DNA data storage, and prior work has analyzed code sizes under synthesis-time constraints but not the minimum synthesis time for codes of a given size.
method: The authors derive finite-length lower bounds valid for arbitrary reference sequences and upper bounds using q-ary differential VT codes, then analyze asymptotic regimes for prescribed code sizes.
result: For certain code sizes they determine the minimum synthesis time up to an O(1) term, compute the redundancy, and show that single-deletion correcting codes require synthesis time exceeding unrestricted codes by a term proportional to log n whose coefficient is determined; they also give bounds and existence conditions for other code sizes.
conclusion: The results quantify how code size and single-deletion correction constraints affect synthesis time, providing theoretical guidance for cost-constrained DNA storage codes.

title: A Proof Of The Constant-width Numerical Range Conjecture
authors: Muyan Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the conjecture of Chien, Nakazato, and Meng that the numerical range of a finite complex matrix has constant width [MATH] if and only if it is a closed disk of radius [MATH], with a singleton allowed when [MATH]. For [MATH], the characteristic polynomial of the associated Hermitian pencil and its translate by [MATH] have a nonconstant common divisor over [MATH]. At points on the unit circle where the factorization can be evaluated, every root of the common divisor equals the smallest eigenvalue. A coefficient of the divisor thus gives a rational formula for that eigenvalue. The characteristic equation forces this rational function to be a Laurent polynomial with exponents in [MATH]. Antipodal symmetry then makes the midpoint of the extreme eigenvalues a first harmonic, giving the support function of a disk. We also obtain the corresponding quadratic factor of the Kippenhahn polynomial.
tldr: The paper proves the Chien–Nakazato–Meng conjecture characterizing finite complex matrices whose numerical range has constant width as closed disks of fixed radius.
motivation: The constant-width numerical range conjecture was an open problem in matrix analysis concerning the geometric structure of numerical ranges.
method: The proof analyzes the characteristic polynomial of the associated Hermitian pencil, its common divisors, factorization on the unit circle, Laurent polynomial structure, and antipodal symmetry of extreme eigenvalues.
result: It establishes that constant-width numerical range implies a closed disk of radius 1/2, with singleton allowed in a degenerate case, and also identifies the corresponding quadratic factor of the Kippenhahn polynomial.
conclusion: The conjecture is resolved, providing a complete geometric characterization of constant-width numerical ranges for finite complex matrices.

title: Banach Isomorphism Between Separable \(L_p\)-spaces, \(1\le P\ne2<\infty\), Associated With Hyperfinite Type Iii Von Neumann Algebras
authors: Chenhao Gao, Jinghao Huang, Yunpeng Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For each fixed \(p\in[1,\infty)\setminus\{2\}\), the number of Banach isomorphism classes of separable \(L_p\)-spaces associated with hyperfinite type III von Neumann algebras is \(2^{\aleph_0}\).
tags: hyperfinite type III von Neumann algebras
tldr: The paper classifies separable L_p-spaces associated with hyperfinite type III von Neumann algebras up to Banach isomorphism, showing there are continuum many isomorphism classes for each fixed p ≠ 2.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the Banach-space structure of noncommutative L_p-spaces arising from hyperfinite type III von Neumann algebras.
method: The work uses Banach-space isomorphism invariants and classification techniques for separable noncommutative L_p-spaces associated with hyperfinite factors.
result: For each p in [1,∞) excluding 2, the number of Banach isomorphism classes is 2^{aleph_0}.
conclusion: The classification reveals a rich continuum-sized family of non-isomorphic separable L_p-spaces in the hyperfinite type III setting, outside the Hilbert-space case p=2.
keywords: hyperfinite type III von Neumann algebras

title: First-order Asymptotic Expansions For Spectral Convergence Of Normalized Graph Laplacians Constructed From Samples On Manifolds
authors: Wolfgang Polonik Eunseong Bae
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under i.i.d. uniform sampling from a closed Riemannian manifold embedded in Euclidean space, we derive first-order asymptotic expansions for the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of symmetrically normalized graph Laplacians constructed via Gaussian kernels and provide concentration inequalities for the remainder terms. As a direct consequence, we establish the corresponding weak convergence results. Unlike most related works, our analysis does not impose a multiplicity-one assumption on the eigenvalues, thereby extending the applicability of the framework to general manifolds with potentially nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.
tldr: The paper derives first-order asymptotic expansions for eigenvalues and eigenvectors of Gaussian-kernel normalized graph Laplacians built from i.i.d. samples on a Riemannian manifold, with concentration bounds for remainder terms and weak convergence results.
motivation: Graph Laplacians are widely used in manifold learning and spectral data analysis, but existing asymptotic analyses often assume simple eigenvalues, limiting applicability to manifolds with eigenvalue multiplicities.
method: Under uniform i.i.d. sampling from a closed embedded Riemannian manifold, the authors analyze symmetrically normalized graph Laplacians with Gaussian kernels and establish first-order eigenvalue/eigenvector expansions plus concentration inequalities without a multiplicity-one assumption.
result: They obtain asymptotic expansions and remainder concentration bounds, yielding weak convergence of the spectral quantities to their continuum manifold counterparts even with nontrivial eigenvalue multiplicities.
conclusion: The work extends spectral convergence theory for graph Laplacians to more general manifolds, but it is a mathematical statistics/manifold-learning contribution with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Robustness Of Controllability Scores For Stable Linear Network Systems
authors: Kazuhiro Sato Ritsuki Yamada
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Controllability scores quantify node importance in linear network systems by optimizing the allocation of input strength. Although the volumetric controllability score (VCS) and average-energy controllability score (AECS) are uniquely defined for Hurwitz systems, their sensitivity to perturbations of the system matrix remains unclear. In this paper, we investigate the robustness of these scores to such perturbations. We first prove that both scores are locally Lipschitz continuous in the system matrix and establish a robustness bound for Hurwitz comparison matrices. We then characterize the directional derivative of the optimal allocation along a differentiable matrix path as the unique solution of a critical-cone quadratic program, whose linear term is computed using differentiated Lyapunov equations. For single-edge weakening, the norm of the resulting response vector provides a robustness-based measure of edge importance. Numerical experiments show that the response, and hence the edge importance, depends on both the criterion and the dynamics, not only on the network topology.
tldr: The paper analyzes the robustness of volumetric and average-energy controllability scores in stable linear network systems under perturbations to the system matrix.
motivation: Controllability scores are used to rank node importance in linear networks, but their sensitivity to perturbations of the system matrix was previously unclear.
method: The authors prove local Lipschitz continuity of both scores, derive robustness bounds for Hurwitz comparison matrices, and characterize directional derivatives via a critical-cone quadratic program using differentiated Lyapunov equations.
result: For single-edge weakening, the response vector norm gives a robustness-based edge-importance measure, and numerical experiments show edge importance depends on both criterion and dynamics, not only topology.
conclusion: The controllability scores are robust in a Lipschitz sense, and their perturbation response provides a criterion-dependent measure of edge importance in linear network systems.

title: When Proofs Are Abundant, What Is A Paper For?
authors: Charles-Albert Lehalle
abstract: ArXiv:2611.12943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems now produce formally verified proofs of celebrated open problems, and the cost of obtaining a correct proof is falling toward zero. If correctness becomes cheap, what is left for a research paper to communicate? I argue that a paper is not exhausted by a verified statement. It is a narrative exposed to the criticism of a community, made of an intension (the author's choice of problem and perspective), a scientific chain of thought (the reasoning steps leading to the result), and the arguments supporting each step. Most published mathematics is judged on these two elements rather than on correctness alone, and machine-generated formal scripts convey neither. Borrowing from logic and type theory, I formalise the first as a Derivation-Level Intension and the second as a Directional Extension: a decomposition of a proof into cut-points whose axiomatic footprints reveal its weak links, where the result could be strengthened, and its strong links, which can be transported to other theories. Moreover, I examine five roles AI can play in the research process, including bibliographical search and critical judgment, and show that none of them removes the need to declare these two elements. I mention ways these two concepts could be useful for Journals and for training of young mathematicians in a AI era. If proofs become abundant, the scarce resource is not correctness but a community's shared understanding of why a result matters and how it could be pushed further.
tldr: A position paper arguing that when AI can produce formally verified proofs cheaply, the value of a research paper lies in its narrative: the author's intension and the reasoning chain, not mere correctness.
motivation: AI systems now generate formally verified proofs of open problems, driving the cost of correctness toward zero, which raises the question of what scientific papers are actually for.
method: Conceptual/philosophical argument borrowing from logic and type theory to formalize two notions — a 'Derivation-Level Intension' (choice of problem and perspective) and a 'Directional Extension' (decomposition of a proof into cut-points revealing weak and strong links) — plus an examination of five roles AI can play in research.
result: The author claims that machine-generated formal scripts convey neither the intension nor the scientific chain of thought, and that these two elements remain necessary regardless of which AI roles are adopted.
conclusion: If proofs become abundant, the scarce resource is not correctness but a community's shared understanding of why a result matters and how it can be extended; these concepts may help journals and the training of young mathematicians.

title: Constant Query LCCs Over The Reals
authors: Zeev Dvir
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note describes a new construction, found by ChatGPT Astra, of constant query Locally Correctable Codes (LCCs) over the real numbers. Prior constructions of constant query LCCs were exclusive to fields of positive characteristic and were conjectured not to exist over the reals. The construction uses low degree polynomial evaluations over an integer grid, together with a novel sampling procedure which outputs, for a given grid point [MATH], a random quadratic curve through [MATH] which intersects the grid in many other points (the decoding queries). The sampler is `smooth' in the sense that no grid point is queried with high probability. These codes have the additional property that the queried locations (the curve/grid intersections) are all nearby grid points.
tldr: A new construction of constant-query locally correctable codes over the real numbers, using low-degree polynomial evaluations on an integer grid with a smooth quadratic-curve sampler.
motivation: Prior constant-query LCC constructions existed only over fields of positive characteristic and were conjectured impossible over the reals, so the paper aims to refute that conjecture.
method: Codewords are evaluations of low-degree polynomials over an integer grid; decoding queries a random quadratic curve through the given point, which intersects the grid in many nearby points, with a smoothness property bounding per-point query probability.
result: The construction yields constant-query LCCs over the reals with locality-preserving structure, where queried locations are nearby grid points and no point is queried with high probability.
conclusion: The conjecture that constant-query LCCs cannot exist over the reals is false, opening a new regime for locally decodable/correctable code constructions over characteristic zero.

title: Moai: Module-Optimizing Architecture For Non-interactive Secure Transformer Inference
authors: Linru Zhang, Xiangning Wang, Jun Jie Sim, Zhicong Huang, Jiahao Zhong, Huaxiong Wang, Pu Duan, Kwok-Yan Lam
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy concerns have been raised in Large Language Models (LLM) inference when models are deployed in Cloud Service Providers (CSP). Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution by enabling secure inference directly over encrypted inputs. However, the high computational overhead of HE remains a major bottleneck. To address this challenge, we propose MOAI, an efficient HE-based, non-interactive framework for secure transformer inference. MOAI gains significant efficiency improvement from: (1) a novel evaluation flow that combines column and diagonal packing with consistent strategies across all layers, eliminating expensive format conversions. (2) rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm that significantly reduce the number of costly HE rotations, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference. (3) Column packing removes rotations in plaintext-ciphertext matrix multiplications and interleaved batching further reduces the rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations compared to the state-of-the-art works across all matrix multiplications of BERT-base. As a result, we achieve a [MATH] reduction in evaluation time compared to the state-of-the-art HE-based non-interactive secure transformer inference, THOR (Moon et al., CCS 25). We then apply MOAI on the Powerformer's framework and achieve a [MATH] reduction in evaluation time compared to Powerformer (Park et al., ACL 25), which approximates Softmax and LayerNorm with simpler functions in transformer and proposes HE-based non-interactive transformer inference. We report an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU environment. We show the extendibility by applying MOAI in LLaMA-3-8B. Our implementation is publicly available as open source.
tldr: MOAI is a homomorphic-encryption-based framework for non-interactive secure transformer inference that cuts the number of costly HE rotations through packed evaluation and rotation-free Softmax/LayerNorm.
motivation: Privacy concerns when LLMs are outsourced to cloud providers motivate secure inference, but homomorphic encryption is dominated by rotation and format-conversion overhead.
method: The authors combine column and diagonal packing under a consistent layer-wise evaluation flow, introduce rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm, and use interleaved batching to reduce rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix products.
result: MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations than prior work on BERT-base, reduces evaluation time relative to THOR and Powerformer, achieves 2.36 minutes amortized per input on one GPU, and extends to LLaMA-3-8B.
conclusion: Careful packing and algorithmic redesign of normalization layers make HE-based non-interactive transformer inference substantially more practical, though the work remains classical applied cryptography.

title: Local Modifications Of Nearest-Neighbor And Min-Plus Representations
authors: Liliia Redina
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how changing a Boolean-valued function at [MATH] inputs affects the size and precision of its exact representations. Starting from a representation of size [MATH], we prove four bounds, two for nearest-neighbor (NN) representations and two for integer min-plus representations. (i) For NN representations on a finite subset of [MATH] with [MATH], at most [MATH] anchors suffice. The coefficient [MATH] is optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of anchors from one to three. (ii) For NN representations on the Boolean cube with rational anchors, let [MATH] be the maximum original coordinate bit length, and let [MATH] be the maximum bit length of the least common denominator of any one original anchor's coordinates. We construct a representation with at most [MATH] anchors on a common dyadic grid and coordinate bit length [MATH]. (iii) For integer min-plus representations on the Boolean cube, we give a construction that keeps the original [MATH] forms and their labels and adds at most [MATH] new forms. Its maximum weight is at most [MATH], where [MATH] is the largest absolute original coefficient, including constant terms. (iv) For integer min-plus representations on a finite rational domain [MATH], at most [MATH] forms suffice. Their maximum weight is polynomially bounded in [MATH], the coordinate bound, and the common denominator of [MATH]. The coefficient [MATH] is again optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of forms from one to three. These bounds imply stability under polynomially many changes on the cube for polynomial-size representations, including those with polynomially bounded NN coordinate bit length or min-plus weight.
tldr: The paper proves bounds on how much the size and precision of nearest-neighbor and integer min-plus representations of Boolean functions degrade when the function is modified at a small number of inputs.
motivation: Representations of Boolean functions by nearest-neighbor (Voronoi) and min-plus (tropical) forms are used in computational geometry, circuit complexity, and learning theory; it is natural to ask whether such representations are stable under local perturbations of the target function.
method: Starting from a given exact representation of size s, the author gives explicit constructions of new representations after changing values at k inputs, bounding the number of anchors/forms, coordinate bit lengths, and weights, and shows the linear-in-k coefficient is optimal via a three-point counterexample.
result: Four bounds are established: NN representations require at most s+k anchors on finite domains (and controlled anchor count and bit length on the Boolean cube with rational anchors), while integer min-plus representations keep the original s forms and add at most k new forms with polynomially bounded weights; the s+k scaling is tight in both settings.
conclusion: Polynomial-size NN and min-plus representations are stable under polynomially many local changes, giving robustness guarantees for representation size and precision under function perturbation.

title: Feedback Vertex Set, Max Cut, And Edge Coloring On The Strong Product Of A Graph And A Path
authors: Jan Diester, Kolja K\"uhn, Manuel Rapp, Samuel Schneider, Torsten Ueckerdt
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine the computational complexity of well-known problems on subgraphs of the strong product of two paths. Namely, for Max Cut we show NP-hardness on induced subgraphs of [MATH] answering a question by Dvo\'ak, Huynh, Joret, Liu, and Wood (2021). For 3-Edge Coloring we show NP-hardness on subgraphs of [MATH] and that it is equivalent to 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs for induced subgraphs of [MATH]. It is a long standing open question whether 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs is NP-hard. As a second contribution, we consider graphs of the form [MATH] and show that Feedback Vertex Set on these graphs is FPT in the clique-width of [MATH]. Furthermore, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if [MATH] is chordal or co-comparable and that the computational complexity depends on the parity of [MATH] if [MATH] is bipartite. Namely, it is solvable in polynomial time if [MATH] has an even number of vertices but is NP-complete otherwise. For Max Cut, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if [MATH] is bipartite.
tldr: This paper studies the computational complexity of Max Cut, 3-Edge Coloring, and Feedback Vertex Set on subgraphs of strong products of a graph with a path.
motivation: The authors aim to resolve open complexity questions, including a question by Dvořák, Huynh, Joret, Liu, and Wood (2021) on Max Cut and the long-standing open problem of whether 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs is NP-hard.
method: They prove NP-hardness reductions for Max Cut and 3-Edge Coloring on induced subgraphs of strong products of paths, and analyze parameterized and polynomial-time solvability of Feedback Vertex Set via clique-width, chordality, and parity arguments.
result: Max Cut is NP-hard on induced subgraphs of the product, 3-Edge Coloring is NP-hard and equivalent to the planar case, and Feedback Vertex Set is FPT in clique-width, polynomial for chordal/co-comparable graphs, and parity-dependent for bipartite graphs.
conclusion: The work settles several open complexity questions in structural graph theory but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Minimal Intuitionistic Public Announcement Logic
authors: Philippe Balbiani, Hans van Ditmarsch, Cigdem Gencer, Clara Lerouvillois
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce intuitionistic public announcement logics Lmin and Lequ determined by classes of birelational frames where the intuitionistic preorder and the modal accessibility relation do not need to satisfy the confluence conditions traditionally considered within the framework of IPAL. Our logics can be seen as generalisations of IPAL seeing that their language is based on a binary epistemic modality of "relativised knowledge" that allows us to define valid reduction axioms. Our main results are the soundness and completeness of Lmin with respect to the class of all birelational frames and the soundness and completeness of Lequ with respect to the class of all birelational frames where the modal accessibility relation is an equivalence relation.
tldr: The paper introduces minimal intuitionistic public announcement logics Lmin and Lequ based on birelational frames without traditional confluence conditions.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize intuitionistic public announcement logic (IPAL) by relaxing standard confluence constraints between the intuitionistic preorder and modal accessibility relation.
method: They define birelational semantics with a binary epistemic modality for relativised knowledge and prove soundness and completeness for Lmin over all birelational frames and for Lequ over frames where the accessibility relation is an equivalence relation.
result: The logics are shown to be sound and complete with respect to their intended classes of frames, and they support valid reduction axioms.
conclusion: This work extends the logical foundations of public announcement logic in an intuitionistic setting, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Everything In Its Right Place: Attention Is A Radio Head
authors: Llu\'is Arola-Fern\'andez, Aissam Khadraoui, Alex Arenas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention, the core of language models, is a digital calculation over tokens: an exponential selects them, a division normalizes and a positional code sets the order. We show that attention can instead emerge from the synchronization of a receiver with its context tokens. Each past token is an oscillator whose state carries its content and whose frequency drifts with its age. The present token selects them by content, aligning an antenna with its query, and by position, setting the frequency of a receiver with its dial. Solving Kuramoto's problem for this receiver yields an attention layer in closed form with two phases: above a critical coupling set by the context, the receiver locks and its weights normalize; below it, it stays silent and its weights sum to less than one. Trained networks use both phases to select, abstain and count, fail where the theory predicts and keep reading far beyond the training length. Each part of attention finds its place in one device, a radio head: it tunes in to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is on air.
tldr: The authors reinterpret transformer attention as a synchronization phenomenon, showing that a Kuramoto-type oscillator receiver locking onto age-dependent context oscillators yields attention in closed form.
motivation: Attention is normally understood as a purely digital computation (softmax selection, normalization, positional encoding); the authors ask whether it can instead emerge from physical synchronization dynamics between a receiver and its context.
method: Each past token is modeled as an oscillator carrying content in its state and drifting frequency with age; solving the Kuramoto problem for a query-driven receiver gives a closed-form attention layer with a locked (normalized) phase above a critical coupling and a silent (sub-normalized) phase below it.
result: Trained networks exploit both phases to select, abstain and count, fail precisely where the theory predicts, and generalize to sequence lengths far beyond training.
conclusion: All components of attention map onto a single 'radio head' device that tunes to what to hear and when, and stays silent when nothing relevant is present.

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument For Bit-Exact Inference Of Large Language Models
authors: Tomer Solberg
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: [URL].
tldr: Sable is a cryptographic argument system and single-GPU prover that certifies bit-exact inference of integer-quantized large language models, achieving proofs for a 32B-parameter transformer in roughly 90-400 seconds.
motivation: Verifying that a committed model actually produced a claimed output is important for trust in open-weight LLM serving, but floating-point nondeterminism and the scale of modern transformers make succinct verifiable inference difficult.
method: The authors fix an integer-only function F_O with deterministic rounding, softmax and sampling, encode it in a constraint system over the 31-bit KoalaBear prime with provable absence of modular wraparound, and batch zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into per-domain sumchecks, committing to all witness tensors via Reed-Solomon/BaseFold multilinear commitments with BLAKE3 Merkle trees, streaming layers on one GPU.
result: On an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s (4,096 tokens) and 398 s (16,384 tokens), is 40-64x faster per parameter-token than zkLLM, costs 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request, and yields round-by-round soundness error 2^-103 in the random-oracle model with 86.3% greedy-token agreement with BF16.
conclusion: Sable demonstrates practical, non-zero-knowledge succinct proofs of bit-exact LLM inference, targeting open-weight models where transparency is acceptable rather than privacy.

title: Evolution Of Cooperation In Enterprise Resource-sharing Networks With Dynamic Participation And Adaptive Decision-making
authors: Pengfei Liu, Bin Pi, Qin Li, Minyu Feng, Attila Szolnoki
abstract: ArXiv:2611.12962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resource sharing among enterprises is an important mechanism for improving resource utilization efficiency and facilitating collaborative development. However, the emergence and sustainability of cooperative behavior depend critically on whether enterprises choose to participate in resource-sharing activities and how they balance cooperation and competition in their decision-making processes. To investigate these issues, we develop an evolutionary cooperation model on the enterprise resource-sharing network that integrates participation status, decision-making modes, and cooperative strategies within a unified framework. Specifically, enterprises dynamically switch between active and dormant states according to their aspiration levels, while Q-learning is employed to enable adaptive selection between payoff-driven and conformist decision-making modes. Meanwhile, interactions between resource-sharing and non-sharing in active enterprises are characterized by the snowdrift game. Through extensive simulations, we systematically examine the effects of the payoff parameter, the reinforcement-learning parameters, the participation and Q-learning mechanism, and network size on enterprise participation and the evolution of cooperation. The results show that an intermediate aspiration level is most favorable for sustaining enterprise participation and facilitating the emergence of cooperation. Moreover, the dynamic activation mechanism effectively mitigates the decline in cooperation under high cost-to-benefit ratios, allowing the system to sustain a decent level of cooperative behavior. These findings highlight the important roles of dynamic participation and adaptive decision-making in shaping the evolution of resource-sharing cooperation and provide a new modeling framework to understand the emergence and persistence of cooperation in complex enterprise networks.
tldr: The paper models the evolution of cooperation among enterprises in resource-sharing networks where firms dynamically switch between active and dormant states and use Q-learning to adaptively choose between payoff-driven and conformist decision-making modes.
motivation: Resource sharing among enterprises improves utilization efficiency, but sustaining cooperative behavior depends on participation choices and on how firms balance cooperation against competition when making decisions.
method: An evolutionary cooperation model is built on an enterprise resource-sharing network combining participation status, decision-making modes, and cooperative strategies, with aspiration-level-driven active/dormant switching, Q-learning for mode selection, and snowdrift-game interactions between sharing and non-sharing active firms, studied via extensive simulation.
result: An intermediate aspiration level best sustains participation and fosters cooperation, and the dynamic activation mechanism mitigates the decline of cooperation under high cost-to-benefit ratios, maintaining a decent cooperative level.
conclusion: Dynamic participation and adaptive decision-making play key roles in shaping resource-sharing cooperation, and the framework offers a new modeling approach for understanding the emergence and persistence of cooperation in complex enterprise networks.

title: The Supercritical Ten Martini Problem
authors: Lingrui Ge, Svetlana Jitomirskaya, Jiangong You
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We solve the ten martini problem for the positive-Lyapunov part of the spectrum of any nonconstant real analytic one-frequency Schr\"odinger operator. The proof uses the intrinsic symplectic structure of the dual center of Ge--Jitomirskaya [28] and extends the Kotani--almost-reducibility strategy of Ge--Jitomirskaya--You [30] from two-dimensional centers to arbitrary finite center dimension.
tldr: The authors solve the ten martini problem for the positive-Lyapunov part of the spectrum of any nonconstant real analytic one-frequency Schrödinger operator.
motivation: The ten martini problem—whether the spectrum of an almost Mathieu-type operator is a Cantor set—has been a central open question in quasi-periodic spectral theory, and prior approaches only handled low-dimensional centers.
method: The proof exploits the intrinsic symplectic structure of the dual center introduced by Ge–Jitomirskaya and extends the Kotani almost-reducibility strategy of Ge–Jitomirskaya–You from two-dimensional centers to arbitrary finite center dimension.
result: The Cantor structure of the spectrum (no intervals) is established throughout the positive-Lyapunov region for general nonconstant real analytic one-frequency potentials.
conclusion: The work settles a long-standing problem in the spectral theory of quasi-periodic Schrödinger operators and provides a general framework for higher-dimensional center analyses.

title: Optimality Guarantees For Minimum Variance Subset Selection Via Semidefinite Programming
authors: Daniel Aloise Antonio M. Sudoso
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a set of data points in Euclidean space and a prescribed cardinality [MATH], the minimum variance [MATH]-subset problem asks for [MATH] points minimizing their average squared distance from their centroid. We develop a semidefinite programming (SDP) framework for exact recovery and global optimization. First, we show that the natural SDP relaxation fails Slater's condition. Identifying the proper face containing its feasible region yields an equivalent, lower-dimensional, strictly feasible formulation that enjoys strong duality. A primal--dual characterization of optimality then gives geometric necessary and sufficient conditions under which the SDP relaxation is guaranteed to be tight. These conditions reveal how tightness depends on the internal geometry of the selected subset and on its separation from the remaining points. Second, we embed the SDP relaxation in a branch-and-cut algorithm combining first-order optimization, valid inequalities and dimension-reducing branching. Extensive experiments on public data sets, with up to 1,500 points and different values of [MATH], show that the method strongly outperforms general-purpose exact solvers as the number of points and cardinality increase.
tldr: This paper develops a semidefinite programming framework with optimality guarantees and a branch-and-cut algorithm for the classical minimum-variance subset selection problem in Euclidean space.
motivation: Selecting a fixed-cardinality subset of points that minimizes average squared distance to its centroid (a clustering-type objective) is a hard combinatorial problem, and the authors aim to provide exact recovery guarantees and a globally optimal solver.
method: They analyze the natural SDP relaxation, show it fails Slater's condition, restrict to the proper face to obtain a strictly feasible lower-dimensional formulation with strong duality, derive primal-dual geometric tightness conditions, and embed the relaxation in a branch-and-cut algorithm with first-order optimization, valid inequalities, and dimension-reducing branching.
result: Experiments on public datasets with up to 1,500 points show the method substantially outperforms general-purpose exact solvers as the number of points and cardinality grow.
conclusion: The work provides both theoretical tightness characterizations and a practical exact solver for minimum-variance subset selection, but it is purely a classical optimization contribution.

title: On Isomorphic Embeddings Of Noncommutative Lorentz Spaces
authors: Chenhao Gao, Jinghao Huang, Fedor Sukochev, Zhizheng Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13631v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is shown that for [MATH], the Lorentz operator ideal [MATH] embeds isomorphically into [MATH] if and only if (1) [MATH] or (2) [MATH] and [MATH], which is in contrast to the classical result that [MATH] embeds into [MATH] as a (complemented) subspace. We also study the isomorphic embeddings between operator ideals generated by the weighted Lorentz sequence spaces [MATH] ([MATH]). We characterize those (commutative/noncommutative) Lorentz function spaces [MATH] that are isomorphic to subspaces of noncommutative [MATH]-spaces for [MATH] over some noncommutative probability spaces, which is a noncommutative version of Sch\"utt's theorem.
tldr: The paper characterizes isomorphic embeddings of noncommutative Lorentz operator ideals into noncommutative Lp-spaces, extending Schütt's theorem to the operator-space setting.
motivation: The work is motivated by classical results on isomorphic embeddings of Lorentz spaces into Lp-spaces and seeks a noncommutative analogue for operator ideals and noncommutative probability spaces.
method: The authors use Banach space geometry and noncommutative functional analysis to study isomorphic embeddings between Lorentz operator ideals and noncommutative Lp-spaces, including weighted Lorentz sequence space constructions.
result: They prove a complete characterization of when a Lorentz operator ideal embeds isomorphically into another, showing conditions that contrast with the classical commutative case, and characterize Lorentz function spaces isomorphic to subspaces of noncommutative Lp-spaces.
conclusion: The paper provides a noncommutative version of Schütt's theorem and clarifies the isomorphic embedding structure of noncommutative Lorentz ideals, though it is a pure functional analysis contribution with no direct quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, or hybrid systems focus.

title: Domain-Invariant And Language-Model-Assisted Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks On Keyboards
authors: Bikrant Bikram Pratap Maurya
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) recover typed text from the sound of keystrokes, using only a commodity microphone and no access to the victim's device. Prior work establishes that such attacks succeed under idealized laboratory conditions - a single keyboard, a fixed microphone, a quiet room, and training and testing on the same device but leaves open the question that matters for security: whether keystroke inference survives the open world of unseen keyboards, diverse users, noisy environments, and compressed transmission channels. The answer developed here is that it does, provided the acoustic model is made explicitly domain-invariant and its noisy predictions are corrected by a language model.
tldr: The paper shows that acoustic keystroke side-channel attacks can generalize beyond controlled lab settings by combining domain-invariant acoustic representations with language-model-based correction of noisy predictions.
motivation: Prior acoustic side-channel work only demonstrated keystroke recovery under idealized conditions (one keyboard, fixed microphone, quiet room, same-device training/testing), leaving open whether such attacks survive unseen keyboards, diverse users, noisy rooms, and compressed audio channels.
method: The author builds an acoustic keystroke classifier trained with explicit domain-invariance objectives to generalize across keyboards, users, and recording conditions, then post-processes its per-keystroke probability outputs with a language model to correct errors and reconstruct coherent text.
result: Keystroke inference is reported to remain effective in the open-world setting of unseen keyboards, varied users, noisy environments, and compressed transmission channels, with language-model correction substantially improving text recovery.
conclusion: Acoustic side-channel keylogging is a practical, generalizable threat rather than a lab curiosity, implying that keyboards and audio channels require defensive attention; the approach is entirely classical machine learning and signal processing.

title: Adversarial Risk Analysis With Fully Probabilistic Designs
authors: Mario Chac\'on-Falc\'on, Tatiana Valentine Guy, Miroslav K\'arn\'y, David Rios Insua
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial risk analysis (ARA) informs decision-makers when facing intelligent opponents and uncertain outcomes, enabling an analyst to model beliefs about the opponents' preferences, capabilities, beliefs, and the strategic calculations that opponents employ. Major applications cover reliability and risk analysis of critical infrastructures in presence of adversarial threats. In such domains, ARA mitigates typical common knowledge assumptions of standard game-theoretic approaches. However, ARA entails complex modelling and computations. To alleviate these, we explore its combination with fully probabilistic design (FPD), a control theory methodology supporting an agent in choosing the decision distribution that achieves the outcomes with a distribution closest to its ideal. We use FPD to model and forecast the opponent's decisions within an ARA setting and present how to handle security games within this ARA-FPD framework, covering both single and multiple stage problems.
tldr: The paper combines adversarial risk analysis (ARA) with fully probabilistic design (FPD) to model and forecast the decisions of intelligent opponents in security-related decision problems.
motivation: ARA avoids the unrealistic common-knowledge assumptions of classical game theory but is computationally and modelling-intensive, so the authors seek a tractable control-theoretic formalism to represent opponents' belief- and preference-dependent choices.
method: Opponent decision-making is modelled as a probabilistic design problem in which the adversary selects a decision distribution close to an ideal one in the KL-divergence sense, embedded in the ARA framework for single- and multi-stage security games.
result: The ARA-FPD framework yields a structured procedure for forecasting adversarial behaviour and evaluating defensive strategies in one-shot and repeated security scenarios, reducing the modelling burden relative to standard ARA.
conclusion: FPD provides a practical complement to ARA for adversarial decision problems in critical-infrastructure risk analysis, though the work remains entirely within classical decision theory and control.

title: Development Of A Versatile Modular System To Study The Ablation And Plume Expansion In A Thin Film
authors: Renjith Kumar R, Pabitra Kumar Mishra, B R Geethika, Hem C Joshi, Jinto Thomas
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-resolved investigation of laser ablation of thin films requires stable, repeatable, and efficient experimental environment. Conventional approaches often rely on multiple laser-ablation shots acquired at different delay times to reconstruct the temporal evolution of the process, thereby assuming shot-to-shot reproducibility. This work presents a novel modular experimental setup that addresses these challenges and enables a systematic pump--probe study of laser--matter interaction. The setup provides reliable single-pulse measurements with controlled sample positioning inside the high vacuum chamber, as well as integrated data recording, which improves redundancy and ease with which experiments can be performed. Further, the setup serves as an advanced diagnostic tool for investigating the time evolution of laser--matter interactions, ablation dynamics and laser-produced plasmas in a single laser shot, in various configurations with a temporal resolution better than 15 ns. Using this capability, we show that for a fixed ablation geometry, the transient reflectivity and transmission response depends strongly on the probing side, indicating that probing direction is an independent diagnostic variable whose omission can lead to incomplete or misleading picture of the ablation dynamics. This experimental technique can advance the understanding of surface modification and plume expansion, which are relevant to fundamental studies and also for range of applications, including laser cleaning of tokamak viewports and mirrors, pulsed laser deposition (PLD), surface structuring and laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT), among others. The present setup is versatile enough to perform these studies under different ablation configurations without implementing major changes in the experimental configuration.
tldr: The paper presents a modular pump-probe experimental setup for time-resolved single-shot studies of laser ablation and plume expansion in thin films.
motivation: Conventional laser-ablation studies often rely on multiple shots at different delays, assuming shot-to-shot reproducibility, which can obscure single-shot dynamics and reduce reliability.
method: The authors develop a high-vacuum modular system with controlled sample positioning, integrated data recording, and pump-probe diagnostics achieving temporal resolution better than 15 ns, enabling single-pulse measurements under different ablation geometries.
result: Using the setup, they show that transient reflectivity and transmission depend strongly on the probing side for a fixed ablation geometry, indicating that probing direction is an independent diagnostic variable that must be controlled.
conclusion: The versatile setup enables systematic single-shot studies of laser-matter interactions and is relevant to applications such as laser cleaning, PLD, surface structuring, and LIFT, but it is not directly connected to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Revisiting The Dispersions And Quality Factors Of Nanoshell Plasmons
authors: Victoria Zhang Ali Ghorashi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dispersions and quality factors of a metallic nanoshell's plasmons may be readily tuned by varying the thickness of the nanoshell. This is because 1. Thickness determines the hybridization between the two nanoshell boundaries and 2. Thickness affects the electronic surface scattering rate and, therefore, the non-radiative decay rates of the plasmonic resonances. We find that prior theoretical works, focused primarily on the thin-nanoshell and retarded regimes, obtained qualitatively incorrect results for both the plasmonic dispersions and the associated plasmonic quality factors. Some of these errors have been pointed out in subsequent works, though the corrected results have not been reported, to our knowledge. Beyond obtaining the correct results (correct dispersions and quality factors as a function of nanoshell thickness), we scrutinize the assumption (used by many prior works) that Matthiessen's rule may be used to combine the effects of bulk and surface-mediated plasmonic scattering processes. To do so, we extend prior work by Dingle to the nanoshell geometry. Although we find qualitative agreement with the Matthiessen's rule approach, we find that Dingle's theory systematically predicts higher quality factors across the range of nanoshell thicknesses we consider.
tldr: The paper revisits plasmon dispersions and quality factors in metallic nanoshells, correcting prior theoretical results and comparing Matthiessen's rule with an extension of Dingle's theory.
motivation: Prior theoretical works on nanoshell plasmons, especially in thin-shell and retarded regimes, reportedly produced qualitatively incorrect dispersions and quality factors, and the corrected results have not been systematically reported.
method: The authors calculate plasmon dispersions and quality factors as functions of nanoshell thickness, scrutinize the use of Matthiessen's rule for combining bulk and surface scattering, and extend Dingle's theory to the nanoshell geometry.
result: They obtain corrected thickness-dependent plasmon dispersions and quality factors, find qualitative agreement with the Matthiessen's rule approach, and show that Dingle's theory systematically predicts higher quality factors across the considered thickness range.
conclusion: The work clarifies and corrects the theory of nanoshell plasmon resonances and scattering, but it is a classical plasmonics/nanophotonics study with no direct connection to the researcher's quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems interests.

title: Non-Gaussian Limit Distributions Of Giant-component Sizes In Inhomogeneous Networks
authors: Takehisa Hasegawa Tomoaki Nogawa
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate that the size distribution of giant components in percolation and epidemic spreading models on highly inhomogeneous networks often fails to converge to a Gaussian distribution in the thermodynamic limit. Instead, when appropriately scaled, the distribution converges to a non-Gaussian limit distribution (NGLD). This scaling behavior aligns with the generalized central limit theorem (GCLT), which governs sums of random variables following heavy-tailed distributions. For scale-free networks, the scaling exponent is determined solely by the degree exponent of the network, independently of the control parameter. In contrast, on the Farey graph, a deterministic hierarchical small-world network, the scaling exponent varies continuously with the control parameter.
tldr: The paper shows that giant-component size distributions in percolation and epidemic models on highly inhomogeneous networks can converge to non-Gaussian limit distributions governed by the generalized central limit theorem.
motivation: Standard assumptions often treat giant-component sizes as Gaussian in the thermodynamic limit, but heavy-tailed network inhomogeneity can violate this expectation.
method: The authors analyze percolation and epidemic spreading models on scale-free and hierarchical networks, scaling the giant-component size distribution and comparing its convergence to generalized central limit behavior.
result: For scale-free networks the scaling exponent depends solely on the degree exponent, while for the Farey graph it varies continuously with the control parameter.
conclusion: Giant-component fluctuations in inhomogeneous networks can exhibit non-Gaussian limit laws, requiring generalized central limit theory rather than Gaussian approximations.

title: Explicit Resonance And Bifurcation Of Symmetric Periodic Solutions For Differential Systems With Multiple Distributed Delays
authors: Chungen Liu Huiting He
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the bifurcation of symmetric periodic solutions for differential systems with multiple distributed delays. For general multiple-delay systems with a quadratic potential, we establish a Hamiltonian formulation with a \(P_{n,m}\)-boundary condition and derive explicit Maslov index and nullity formulas. For the special case of two distributed delays, we extend the analysis to general nonlinear potentials. These results yield explicit resonance criteria, bifurcation conditions, and Rabinowitz type and Fadell-Rabinowitz type alternatives for [MATH]-distinct solutions.
tldr: The paper studies symmetric periodic solutions and bifurcations in differential systems with multiple distributed delays using Hamiltonian formulations, Maslov index, and nullity formulas.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize resonance and bifurcation phenomena for delay differential systems with multiple distributed delays and general potentials.
method: They establish a Hamiltonian formulation with P_{n,m}-boundary conditions, derive explicit Maslov index and nullity formulas, and apply these to two-distributed-delay systems with nonlinear potentials.
result: The analysis yields explicit resonance criteria, bifurcation conditions, and Rabinowitz- and Fadell-Rabinowitz-type alternatives for distinct solutions.
conclusion: The work provides a mathematical framework for detecting and classifying symmetric periodic solutions in multi-delay differential systems, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Patch LegONet: Resolving Localized High-Frequency Pde Dynamics With Low-Frequency Operator Blocks
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Junyi Wu, Yueqi Wang, Guang Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Localized interfaces, layers, and shocks can require high spatial resolution even when most of a partial differential equation (PDE) solution remains smooth. In global spectral methods, resolving these features requires increasing the approximation order across the entire domain. LegONet builds PDE solvers from reusable mechanism blocks, but its global coefficient representation faces the same limitation. We introduce Patch LegONet, which reuses pretrained mechanism blocks on smaller physical patches to resolve localized fine scales. The solution consists of a global background and local corrections. Mapping a fixed reference representation onto smaller patches increases local resolution without enlarging the blocks. The corrections join smoothly to the global background at patch boundaries. Differential operators are rescaled analytically to account for each patch's physical size. Nonlinear mechanisms are evaluated on the combined solution to include interactions between the background and local corrections. Patches can move, merge, or be removed during rollout while the pretrained patch blocks remain frozen. Six experiments on Allen-Cahn and viscous Burgers equations assess static, multiple, and moving patches in one to three dimensions. At comparable numbers of degrees of freedom, Patch LegONet consistently lowers the final relative solution error compared with global refinement. The reduction is approximately one order of magnitude in most tests. These results extend mechanism reuse across spatial scales and provide a practical route to local refinement in learned PDE solvers.
tldr: Patch LegONet extends a learned neural operator PDE solver by applying frozen pretrained 'mechanism blocks' on small local patches to resolve localized high-frequency solution features at reduced cost.
motivation: Global spectral and operator-learning representations require uniformly high order to capture localized shocks, layers, and interfaces, which is wasteful when most of the solution is smooth.
method: The solution is decomposed into a global background plus local patch corrections; a fixed reference representation is mapped onto smaller physical patches, differential operators are analytically rescaled per patch, and nonlinear mechanisms are evaluated on the combined solution while patch blocks stay frozen.
result: Across six experiments on Allen-Cahn and viscous Burgers equations in one to three dimensions (static, multiple, and moving patches), final relative error drops by roughly an order of magnitude versus global refinement at comparable degrees of freedom.
conclusion: Mechanism reuse can be extended across spatial scales, offering a practical local-refinement route for learned PDE solvers.

title: Block-Sparse Gauss-Newton Optimization Of Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Sparse Automatic Differentiation Approach
authors: Denis Korolev, Adrian Hill, Jeeeun Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we develop an efficient Gauss-Newton optimization approach for finite basis physics-informed neural networks (FBPINNs). The key ingredient is the overlapping domain decomposition architecture of FBPINNs, which localizes the influence of each subnetwork and induces block sparsity in both the residual Jacobian and the corresponding Gauss-Newton matrix. We characterize this structure and exploit it through sparse automatic differentiation, using graph coloring to partition structurally orthogonal Jacobian columns or rows. This reduces differentiation costs and memory requirements while preserving all structurally nonzero derivative information. The resulting compressed Jacobian representations allow us to assemble the Gauss-Newton system directly in block-sparse form, enabling the use of sparse direct solvers and preconditioned iterative methods. In this way, the otherwise expensive second-order optimization problem is reduced to scalable sparse linear algebra. We demonstrate the approach on multiscale PDEs, where accurate approximation requires rich neural network parametrizations and large numbers of collocation points. Numerical experiments show that our block-sparse Gauss-Newton method attains high accuracy and substantially accelerates optimization relative to first-order baselines while remaining computationally tractable for large problem sizes.
tldr: The paper develops a block-sparse Gauss-Newton optimizer for finite basis physics-informed neural networks by exploiting the overlapping domain decomposition structure to compress Jacobians via graph coloring.
motivation: Second-order optimization of PINNs is expensive in memory and differentiation cost, especially for multiscale PDEs requiring large networks and many collocation points.
method: They characterize the block-sparse structure induced by FBPINN domain decomposition and use graph coloring with sparse automatic differentiation to assemble a block-sparse Gauss-Newton system solvable by sparse direct or preconditioned iterative solvers.
result: Numerical experiments on multiscale PDEs show high accuracy and substantial speedups over first-order baselines while remaining tractable at large problem sizes.
conclusion: Block sparsity plus sparse AD makes Gauss-Newton training of FBPINNs scalable, though the work is purely numerical optimization with no quantum information content.

title: Branching Pattern Modeling: A Geometric Measure Theory Approach
authors: Qinglan Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article is based on a lecture given at Westlake University. It aims to introduce students to an application of geometric measure theory in modeling branched patterns found in both living and nonliving systems. We begin with the Eulerian framework of ramified optimal transportation, including discrete transport paths, their basic properties, numerical approximation, and the passage to general transport paths represented by rectifiable currents. We then describe an application to the dynamic formation of a plant leaf, where branching venation patterns arise from a balance between metabolic benefit and transportation cost. Finally, we review landscape functions associated with transport paths and explain how two existing approaches can be unified within a broader family of rectifiable [MATH]-currents. We conclude by indicating several open directions related to Gilbert-type network problems, biological modeling, and numerical approximation.
tldr: This lecture-style article introduces geometric measure theory methods for modeling branching patterns via ramified optimal transport and rectifiable currents.
motivation: The paper aims to teach students how geometric measure theory can model branched structures in living and nonliving systems, such as plant leaf venation.
method: It develops an Eulerian framework for ramified optimal transportation using discrete transport paths, numerical approximation, and general transport paths represented by rectifiable currents, then applies it to leaf venation and landscape functions.
result: The article reviews and unifies two existing approaches to landscape functions within a broader family of rectifiable currents and identifies open directions in Gilbert-type network problems, biological modeling, and numerical approximation.
conclusion: The work is a pedagogical mathematical modeling review with no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Uniform Symmetric Spectral Finiteness Of Semialgebraic Cones
authors: Mitsuhiro Nishijima
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cone-constrained eigenvalues of a matrix are defined through a complementarity problem constrained by a closed convex cone. We show that every closed semialgebraic convex cone is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite; that is, the cone spectra, the sets of the cone-constrained eigenvalues, of symmetric matrices relative to the cone are uniformly finite with respect to the matrices. The uniform bound is explicit, and as an application, we derive a uniform bound for the cardinality of spectra of symmetric matrices relative to L\"{o}wner cones. In addition, using the uniform finiteness of cone spectra, we also show the uniform finiteness of the number of singular values relative to two closed semialgebraic convex cones. For non-semialgebraic cones, we observe two contrasting phenomena. On the one hand, we show that the exponential cone is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite. On the other hand, we provide a closed non-semialgebraic convex cone such that the associated cone spectra of symmetric matrices are finite but are not uniformly finite.
tldr: The paper proves uniform symmetric spectral finiteness for closed semialgebraic convex cones and derives uniform bounds on cone-constrained eigenvalue and singular-value counts.
motivation: Cone-constrained eigenvalues arise from complementarity problems over convex cones, but it is unclear whether the number of such eigenvalues can be bounded uniformly across matrices for broad classes of cones.
method: The author studies cone spectra of symmetric matrices relative to closed convex cones and uses semialgebraic geometry to establish explicit uniform finiteness bounds, with applications to Löwner cones and singular values relative to two cones.
result: Every closed semialgebraic convex cone is uniformly symmetrically spectrally finite; the exponential cone also has this property, while a closed non-semialgebraic convex cone is constructed whose cone spectra are finite but not uniformly finite.
conclusion: Uniform spectral finiteness holds for semialgebraic cones and some non-semialgebraic cones, but the general non-semialgebraic setting exhibits contrasting behavior.

title: Minimal Dynamics With Polynomial And Intermediate Complexity
authors: Gabriel Lacerda Heric Corr\^ea
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how complicated the orbits of a minimal system can be when the topological entropy vanishes, by looking at the exact order of growth of the number of distinguishable orbit segments, and not only at its exponent. For a broad class of growth rates, including all polynomial ones, we construct minimal homeomorphisms of one-dimensional continua realizing them; in particular, two such systems may have the same polynomial entropy and yet incomparable growth. We also show that passing from a minimal subshift to the maps obtained by running its suspension flow for a fixed time only rescales time in the growth law, and we characterize exactly when this rescaling has no effect. Combined with a construction of Cassaigne, this yields minimal homeomorphisms of continua whose growth lies strictly between all polynomial and all exponential rates.
tldr: The paper studies growth rates of distinguishable orbit segments in minimal systems with vanishing topological entropy and constructs minimal homeomorphisms of one-dimensional continua realizing polynomial and intermediate complexity growth rates.
motivation: The authors aim to refine the classification of zero-entropy minimal systems by examining the exact growth order of orbit-segment counts, not merely whether the exponent is zero.
method: They construct minimal homeomorphisms on one-dimensional continua for a broad class of growth rates, analyze polynomial entropy versus finer growth equivalence, and study time-rescaling effects under suspension flows.
result: They show that systems with the same polynomial entropy can have incomparable growth, characterize when suspension-flow time rescaling leaves the growth law unchanged, and obtain minimal homeomorphisms with growth strictly between polynomial and exponential rates.
conclusion: The work provides finer invariants for minimal zero-entropy dynamics and demonstrates a continuum of intermediate complexity behaviors in one-dimensional minimal systems.

title: A Fast Proximal-Gradient Algorithm For Decentralised Optimisation
authors: Ye Pu, Matthew K Tam, Liam Timms
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a connected multi-agent network where agents coordinate to minimise a finite sum of convex functions. Each function in the sum can be further expressed as the sum of a smooth and nonsmooth component and is known only to a single agent in the network. We propose a decentralised proximal-gradient-type algorithm for solving this problem, which we term Fast PG-EXTRA. In each iteration, agents evaluate the gradient of the smooth component of their local objective functions and the proximal operator of the nonsmooth component, followed by communicating the results with neighbouring agents in the network. Fast PG-EXTRA can be viewed as an accelerated variant of PG-EXTRA, in the sense that it enjoys non-ergodic [MATH] convergence rates in terms of the first-order optimality residual, successive iterates, and consensus error, compared to PG-EXTRA's ergodic [MATH] convergence rates. Our analysis of Fast PG-EXTRA is based on an accelerated variant of the Condat--V\~{u} algorithm for non-distributed convex minimisation, which has similarly improved convergence rates compared to the Condat--V\~{u} algorithm. We validate our convergence results for Fast PG-EXTRA and demonstrate its potential advantages compared to PG-EXTRA with numerical experiments for power state system estimation and [MATH]-regularised logistic regression.
tldr: The paper proposes Fast PG-EXTRA, a decentralized proximal-gradient algorithm for multi-agent convex optimization with non-ergodic convergence rates.
motivation: The authors aim to accelerate decentralized optimization over connected multi-agent networks where each agent knows only its local smooth-plus-nonsmooth convex objective.
method: Fast PG-EXTRA performs local gradient and proximal operator evaluations and neighbor communication, analyzed via an accelerated variant of the Condat-Vu algorithm.
result: The algorithm achieves non-ergodic convergence rates in first-order optimality residual, successive iterates, and consensus error, improving over PG-EXTRA's ergodic rates, with numerical experiments on power system state estimation and L1-regularized logistic regression.
conclusion: Fast PG-EXTRA provides faster convergence for decentralized convex optimization but is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Statistical Analysis Of The Structure From Noise Phenomenon In Generalized Procrustes Problems
authors: Shuyang Ling Jiayang Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), observations are highly noisy, and scientists often use reference templates to guide matching, alignment, and averaging to reconstruct the molecular structure. However, these procedures can produce an output resembling the template even when the observations contain only noise, a phenomenon known as Einstein from noise (EfN). This phenomenon has attracted attention in statistics, where simplified observation models involving group actions have been studied to understand the resulting model bias. Characterizing the bias in the full cryo-EM pipeline remains challenging. We study template matching and averaging in the generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem, which provides an analytically tractable setting involving continuous orthogonal group action and lower-dimensional projections of ordered point clouds. We show that, for pure Gaussian noise, the mean of the aligned-and-averaged estimator admits the same left and right singular-vector bases as the template but its singular values may be distorted. This identifies the subspace structure imposed by the template even in the absence of signal. We characterize the singular values and bound their distortion, establish finite-sample operator-norm bounds, and give sufficient sample sizes for the population mean to dominate random fluctuations. In fact, this bias still exists under weak signals: when the template rank is at least the observation dimension, the change from the pure-noise mean is [MATH] in signal amplitude [MATH]. Our results provide an explicit characterization of model bias in a registration problem motivated by cryo-EM and show why averaging more observations can stabilize structure imposed by the template without removing the bias.
tldr: The paper analyzes template-induced bias in generalized orthogonal Procrustes problems motivated by cryo-EM, showing that averaging noisy observations can reproduce subspace structure from a reference template even without signal.
motivation: Cryo-EM reconstruction pipelines can produce structures resembling reference templates even when observations are pure noise, a phenomenon called Einstein from noise; the authors aim to characterize this model bias analytically.
method: They study template matching and averaging under a generalized orthogonal Procrustes model with Gaussian noise and continuous orthogonal group actions, deriving population mean structure, singular-value distortion bounds, and finite-sample operator-norm guarantees.
result: For pure Gaussian noise, the aligned-and-averaged estimator shares the template's left and right singular-vector bases while its singular values may be distorted; the bias persists under weak signals and averaging more observations stabilizes rather than removes it.
conclusion: The work provides explicit statistical characterization of template-induced bias in a registration problem motivated by cryo-EM, explaining why structure imposed by templates can survive averaging.

title: Fractional-Order Hybrid Sir Forecasting Of Covid-19 In Bangladesh And The United States: Memory Effects And Out-of-Sample Evaluation
authors: Mohammad Shah Alam Md Babul Hossain
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractional-order epidemic models are often justified by memory, yet whether memory improves forecasts is rarely tested out of sample. We extend a hybrid SIR framework, in which a daily transmission rate is reconstructed from reported cases and then forecast, to Caputo fractional order [MATH]. We prove well-posedness, conservation, positivity and a linearized threshold at disease-free states, and derive a Gr\"unwald-Letnikov reconstruction that reduces exactly to the integer-order one at [MATH]. Our main theoretical result shows that for [MATH] the influence of the unknown initial infectious count vanishes, but no faster than [MATH]; after 332 daily steps it is about [MATH] times larger at [MATH] than at [MATH]. In out-of-sample forecasting over 27 weekly origins, the effect of memory depends on the setting. In Bangladesh the integer order gives the lowest error for linear and constant-rate forecasts in 47 of 48 settings. In the United States, where reported cases reached about 18% of the population, a fractional order lowers the linear forecaster's error in all 12 comparisons in 2021 but raises the constant-rate forecaster's, with no difference significant after Holm adjustment. Against standard baselines, the SIR-based linear forecaster was more accurate than the classical SIR model and a neural network without SIR structure, and competitive with ARIMA: in the United States the fractional linear forecaster had the lowest error of all methods (seven-day MAPE 7.54% against 9.14% for ARIMA), whereas in Bangladesh ARIMA had the lowest MAPE, with no significant difference from ARIMA in either country. The choice of a fractional order should rest on out-of-sample evidence rather than in-sample fit.
tldr: The paper evaluates whether Caputo fractional-order memory improves out-of-sample COVID-19 forecasting in a hybrid SIR framework for Bangladesh and the United States.
motivation: Fractional-order epidemic models are often justified by memory effects, but it is rarely tested whether such memory actually improves forecasting performance out of sample.
method: The authors extend a hybrid SIR model with a reconstructed daily transmission rate to Caputo fractional order, prove basic mathematical properties, and compare integer- versus fractional-order forecasts across weekly origins using standard baselines.
result: Fractional order helps in some U.S. linear-forecast settings but generally not in Bangladesh; the SIR-based linear forecaster is competitive with ARIMA and better than classical SIR and a neural network without SIR structure.
