Furthermore, our model predicts that increasing public awareness of congestion can be an effective control strategy to increase utilization of public transit. However, car-centric social norms must be sufficiently small, or car use is instead amplified.
tldr: A compartmental model of urban transit mode choice shows hysteresis between congested and uncongested traffic states and predicts that raising congestion awareness boosts public transit use only when car-centric social norms are weak.
motivation: Traffic congestion arises partly from human mode-choice decisions, and the feedback loop between traffic levels and transit mode choices is poorly understood; the authors aim to characterize it.
method: The authors build a compartmental (SIR-like) model of car, bus, and train mode utilization, first with fixed demand and then with dynamic, choice-dependent demand rates that close the feedback loop between congestion and mode choice.
result: Hysteresis between congested and uncongested regimes persists after adding buses and trains, and relative trip completion rates per mode are derived; feedback redistributes demand across modes, and congestion-awareness campaigns increase transit use provided car-centric social norms remain sufficiently small, otherwise car use is amplified.
conclusion: Traffic conditions are a key driver of mode choice, and awareness-based control policies are effective only below a threshold of car-centric social bias.

title: Aria: An AI-Powered Radio-Channel Inference And Analysis Pipeline
authors: Homa Nikbakht, Mingjun Ying, Dipankar Shakya, Daniel Abraham, Theodore S. Rappaport
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical channel models play a key role in the design and standardization of next-generation wireless systems. The models substitute for costly and time-consuming field measurements when fitted distributions accurately reproduce the measured channel impulse responses. Future wireless systems will operate in global spectrum allocations from 1 to 150 GHz. Over the full span, analytically chosen distribution families fitted to scarce measurement data fail to deliver the required accuracy. Generative AI models instead learn each distribution from the radio-propagation data itself, adapt to the measured structure at every frequency, and scale across the entire band. We present ARIA, an AI-powered Radio-channel Inference and Analysis pipeline that learns each channel-parameter distribution from the measurements. The pipeline extracts power-delay profiles and recovers the channel parameters with time-cluster spatial-lobe (TCSL) analysis. Three neural density estimators, namely mixture density networks, neural spline flows (NSF), and denoising diffusion implicit models, learn each parameter's distribution. A composite rank across goodness-of-fit metrics with Friedman-Nemenyi testing identifies the best estimator, and a maximum-likelihood step anchored to the measured samples converts its density into closed-form parametric families. We instantiate ARIA on the NYU WIRELESS 16.95 GHz InH campaign and find that NSF outperforms the other estimators on every metric. We also show that a conditional NSF with feature-wise linear modulation, trained jointly on the 6.75 and 16.95 GHz measurements, improves over single-frequency training. We feed the fitted distributions into the NYUSIM simulator and reproduce the measured omnidirectional RMS delay spread medians within 2 ns, the per-lobe azimuth and zenith spread medians within 1 degree, and the omnidirectional zenith spread medians within 0.5 degrees.
tldr: ARIA is an AI pipeline that learns radio-channel parameter distributions from propagation measurements using neural density estimators and converts them into closed-form models for wireless simulation.
motivation: Statistical channel models for 1–150 GHz wireless systems require accurate distributional fits, but analytically chosen distribution families fail to capture measured channel structure across the full band, especially with scarce measurement data.
method: The pipeline extracts power-delay profiles, recovers channel parameters via time-cluster spatial-lobe (TCSL) analysis, and fits distributions with mixture density networks, neural spline flows, and denoising diffusion implicit models, selecting the best via a composite goodness-of-fit rank with Friedman-Nemenyi testing and a maximum-likelihood conversion to parametric families.
result: On the NYU WIRELESS 16.95 GHz InH campaign, neural spline flows outperform all other estimators on every metric, and a conditional NSF with FiLM trained jointly at 6.75 and 16.95 GHz beats single-frequency training; NYUSIM simulations reproduce measured delay-spread and angular-spread medians within 2 ns and 1 degree.
conclusion: Generative AI density estimation offers a scalable, measurement-driven alternative to analytic channel models across wide spectrum bands, though the work is purely classical wireless engineering with no quantum information, thermodynamics, networking-quantum, or hybrid-platform relevance.

title: Neumann Series Of Bessel Functions For A Quadratic Sturm--Liouville Pencil
authors: Sergii M. Torba Vladislav V. Kravchenko
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct Neumann series of Bessel functions representations for solutions and their first derivatives of the equation [MATH]. The series arise from Legendre expansions of two transmutation operator kernels. The obtained series converge uniformly on horizontal strips in the complex plane of the parameter [MATH]. We develop a recursive integration procedure for computing the coefficients of these representations. The knowledge of the first coefficients allows one to recover the potentials [MATH] and [MATH] which is useful for solving inverse problems. For separated boundary conditions, we estimate the characteristic functions whose zeros determine the eigenvalues. Two numerical examples illustrate the practical applicability of the obtained series representations to the solution of spectral problems.
tldr: The paper constructs Neumann series of Bessel functions representations for solutions of a quadratic Sturm–Liouville pencil, enabling recovery of potentials and estimation of eigenvalues.
motivation: Transmutation operator methods and Bessel-type series representations provide efficient, uniformly convergent tools for solving spectral and inverse spectral problems for second-order differential equations with polynomial parameter dependence.
method: Legendre expansions of two transmutation kernel functions are used to derive Neumann series of Bessel functions for solutions and their derivatives, together with a recursive procedure for computing the coefficients.
result: The series converge uniformly on horizontal strips of the complex parameter plane; the first coefficients recover the two potentials, and characteristic functions for separated boundary conditions are estimated, illustrated by two numerical examples.
conclusion: The approach yields practical, numerically stable representations useful for spectral and inverse problems of quadratic Sturm–Liouville pencils.

title: Multiscale LegONet: Learning Coefficient-Dependent Local Spaces For Composable Multiscale Finite Elements With Localized Error Bounds
authors: Yueqi Wang, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Guang Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce multiscale LegONet (Ms-LegONet), a plug-and-play learned block for heterogeneous elliptic problems. One network per spatial dimension is trained once on local coefficient patches and reused, without retraining, across coefficient layouts, sources, boundary data and domain sizes within the trained coefficient class. On a fixed primitive patch the network maps the local coefficient to a zero-boundary space, the only learned object. The multiscale basis functions are the harmonic extensions of a fixed set of boundary traces, each a Galerkin solve in that space. Shared interface traces enforce continuity, larger blocks are assembled by recursive static condensation without any parent-scale network, and a localized C\'ea bound attributes the error of the learned spaces primitive by primitive. The training labels are harmonic responses of single patches, so no global solve enters the training. Against MsFEM, GMsFEM, the neural-operator element method and an end-to-end Fourier neural operator, Ms-LegONet is the most accurate at equal unknowns: its [MATH] error is [MATH] to [MATH] times below the baselines on two-dimensional mosaics of [MATH] high-contrast primitives, and its median error stays within [MATH] percentage points of that of exact local spaces in three-dimensional layered media. For each new coefficient it is [MATH] to [MATH] times faster than a fine-grid direct solve in two dimensions. In three dimensions it computes the many-query port response of a chain [MATH] to [MATH] times faster than finite element solves on the same or a finer mesh, at a relative error of [MATH] against their [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: Ms-LegONet is a learned plug-and-play block that constructs multiscale finite element spaces for heterogeneous elliptic problems, with localized Céa error bounds and reuse across coefficient layouts without retraining.
motivation: Multiscale and neural-operator solvers for heterogeneous elliptic PDEs typically require retraining or global solves and lack rigorous localized error control; the authors aim for a reusable, dimension-wise learned local space with per-patch error attribution.
method: One network per spatial dimension is trained on local coefficient patches to map coefficients to a zero-boundary space; multiscale basis functions are harmonic extensions of fixed boundary traces obtained by local Galerkin solves, assembled via recursive static condensation with training labels from single-patch harmonic responses.
result: Against MsFEM, GMsFEM, the neural-operator element method and an end-to-end Fourier neural operator, Ms-LegONet achieves the lowest error at equal unknowns (orders of magnitude lower on 2D high-contrast mosaics) and median errors within a few percent of exact local spaces in 3D layered media, while being substantially faster than fine-grid direct solves.
conclusion: Learned local spaces with localized error bounds offer an accurate, reusable and efficient alternative for multiscale elliptic problems, though the work lies in numerical analysis and scientific machine learning rather than quantum information.

title: Exact (Non-)Accelerations Of Heavy-Ball Discretizations
authors: Martin Tak\'a\v{c} Dmitry Pasechnyuk-Vilensky
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Momentum methods with the same slow dynamics can have different worst-case rates on smooth strongly convex functions. We identify a half-step phase barrier in the gradient query that governs this difference. For momentum with extrapolation [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH], the exact uniform distance factor is [MATH], with [MATH], when [MATH] and [MATH]; [MATH] is the slowest quadratic decay exponent. Quadratically accelerated families with [MATH] have divergent trajectories on the full function class. Upper bounds use finite-lag certificates: nonnegative combinations of inequalities for values and gradients at finitely separated query points, together with comparisons to the minimizer. For any prescribed accuracy, spiral mixtures or quadratic trajectories of one finite-dimensional objective give matching lower bounds at all iteration horizons. We resolve the parameter layer near [MATH] and classify all tunings of this family attaining the optimal leading constant 1. The flow also bounds the leading constant of every second-order stationary linear family with the same slow parameters [MATH] and fixed finite memory.
tldr: The paper identifies a half-step phase barrier in gradient queries that explains why momentum methods with identical slow dynamics can have different worst-case convergence rates on smooth strongly convex functions.
motivation: Momentum (heavy-ball) methods sharing the same slow dynamics nonetheless exhibit different worst-case rates, and the source of this discrepancy was not understood.
method: The authors derive exact uniform distance factors for momentum with extrapolation and prove both upper bounds via finite-lag certificates (nonnegative combinations of value/gradient inequalities) and matching lower bounds via spiral mixtures and quadratic trajectories of finite-dimensional objectives.
result: The exact uniform distance factor is determined, quadratically accelerated families with certain parameters are shown to diverge on the full function class, the parameter layer near the critical point is resolved, and all tunings attaining the optimal leading constant 1 are classified.
conclusion: The half-step phase barrier governs acceleration limits for this family and also bounds the leading constant of every second-order stationary linear family with the same slow parameters and fixed finite memory.

title: BypassGym: A Benchmark For Evaluating Ai Agents' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities
authors: Weifeng Yuan, Zifan Chen, Yucheng Zhang, Feng Dong, Peng Gao, Haoyu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence agents increasingly automate cybersecurity tasks, including offensive operations. Frequent attacks across the web make endpoint detection and response (EDR) a critical defense, but whether AI agents can evade it remains unclear. Benchmarks evaluate the offensive capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents in areas such as penetration testing and vulnerability discovery. One important capability that these benchmarks do not address is defense evasion, specifically whether an agent can develop a program that executes a payload without being blocked or terminated by a deployed EDR. We introduce BypassGym, to our knowledge the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this capability on real endpoints. Given command-and-control (C2) shellcode, an agent must generate and compile a loader that executes the payload without being blocked or terminated. A supplementary evasion knowledge skill provides domain knowledge and supports comparisons with and without this input. BypassGym is built on Proxmox VE(PVE), so the evaluation environment runs real Windows systems and EDR products inside virtual machines and returns structured detection feedback to the agent. We evaluate 5 lightweight model backends against 6 EDR products and 3 payloads, and find that even these simple models generate successful submissions, with DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash reaching 17/18 successful runs and Bitdefender allowing only 5 of 15 runs to pass. These results provide a systematic measurement of current AI agents' endpoint defense evasion capabilities and identify areas for defenders to investigate.
tldr: BypassGym is a benchmark for measuring whether LLM-based agents can generate loaders that execute shellcode payloads without being blocked by real endpoint detection and response (EDR) products.
motivation: AI agents increasingly automate offensive cybersecurity tasks, yet existing benchmarks (penetration testing, vulnerability discovery) do not measure defense evasion, leaving a key capability unquantified for both attackers and defenders.
method: The benchmark runs real Windows systems and six commercial EDR products inside Proxmox VE virtual machines, giving agents structured detection feedback while they iteratively generate and compile loaders around supplied command-and-control shellcode, optionally aided by a supplementary evasion-knowledge skill.
result: Even lightweight model backends produce successful evasions, with DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash achieving 17/18 successful runs, while Bitdefender blocked all but 5 of 15 runs, revealing wide variance across EDR products.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic measurement of current AI agents' endpoint defense evasion capabilities and highlights concrete areas for defenders to investigate.

title: Unified Far-field And Near-field Codebook Design For XL-array Systems
authors: Chao Zhou, Changsheng You, Liujia Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While extremely large-scale antenna arrays (XL-arrays) hold immense promise for next-generation wireless networks, the paradigm shift encompassing new near-field communications renders conventional discrete Fourier transform (DFT)-based Type-I codebooks inefficient. Meanwhile, existing near-field alternatives usually impose prohibitively high storage and/or feedback burdens. To tackle these challenges, we propose in this letter a unified codebook applicable to both far-field and near-field XL-array systems. Our key idea is to express the near-field channel steering vector in an equivalent form, which is a Hadamard product of an angular vector and a curvature-related vector. This new representation allows direct reuse of the legacy Type-I codebook for angle quantization, while only a lightweight auxiliary codebook is newly added for additional curvature quantization. Subsequently, we optimize the auxiliary curvature codebook by maximizing the average beamforming gain given the information of user distribution. By leveraging the local monotonicity of the beamforming gain with respect to curvature mismatch, the optimization problem is further reduced to a quantization-error minimization problem, for which suboptimal curvature codewords are obtained. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed unified codebook achieves near-optimal beamforming performance that approaches its upper bound based on perfect channel state information (CSI), while significantly reducing the required feedback overhead as compared to various benchmark schemes.
tldr: The paper proposes a unified far-field/near-field codebook for extremely large-scale antenna arrays by expressing near-field steering vectors as a Hadamard product of angular and curvature vectors, reusing legacy DFT Type-I codebooks plus a lightweight auxiliary curvature codebook.
motivation: XL-arrays introduce near-field propagation effects that degrade conventional DFT-based Type-I codebooks, while existing near-field alternatives incur high storage and feedback overhead.
method: The near-field steering vector is decomposed into an angular vector and a curvature-related vector, enabling reuse of the Type-I codebook for angle quantization; the auxiliary curvature codebook is then optimized by maximizing average beamforming gain, reduced to a quantization-error minimization problem using local monotonicity of gain versus curvature mismatch.
result: Numerical results show near-optimal beamforming performance approaching the perfect-CSI upper bound while significantly reducing feedback overhead compared to benchmark schemes.
conclusion: The unified codebook offers a low-overhead, backward-compatible solution for both far-field and near-field XL-array systems in next-generation wireless networks.

title: AI-Adaptive Virtual Reality For Stem: Engagement, Retention, And Learning Outcomes
authors: Srinivasa K G, Akshit Rana, Aman Singh, Kshitij Kumar Singh Chauhan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) presents a com pelling opportunity to transform STEM pedagogy; however, empirical evidence evaluating AI-driven adaptivity, objective engagement metrics, and long-term knowledge retention remains sparse. This paper proposes and evaluates an AI-adaptive VR based solar system learning module deployed on Meta Quest 2, wherein a machine learning model dynamically adjusts in structional difficulty based on real-time learner interaction logs including dwell time, gaze patterns, and response latency. A controlled between-subjects experiment was conducted involving 120 secondary school students (mean age 14.3 years) across three schools in India, randomly assigned to three conditions: AI adaptive VR, standard VR, and traditional classroom instruction. Engagement was measured objectively through eye-tracking fixation density and heart rate variability (HRV), alongside pre-test, immediate post-test, and delayed post-tests at one week and one month intervals. Statistical analyses encompassing paired t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) reveal that the AI-adaptive VR cohort demonstrated significantly higher knowledge improvement scores (mean gain = 38.4 vs. 31.2 vs. 10.7), superior one-month retention (p < 0.001), and measurably elevated engagement across all biometric indicators. SEM confirmed immersion as a significant mediator between adaptive instruction and knowledge acquisition ( = 0.63, p < 0.001). Post-session self-directed learning exploration was recorded at 80% among AI-adaptive VR participants versus 40% in the traditional group. These findings establish an evidence based framework for deploying AI-adaptive immersive learning environments in resource-varied STEM educational contexts.
tldr: An AI-adaptive virtual reality solar-system learning module was evaluated with 120 secondary school students in India, showing improved knowledge gains, retention, and biometric engagement versus standard VR and traditional instruction.
motivation: VR offers a promising avenue for STEM pedagogy, but empirical evidence on AI-driven adaptivity, objective engagement measures, and long-term retention is scarce.
method: A between-subjects experiment on Meta Quest 2 compared AI-adaptive VR, standard VR, and classroom instruction, using eye-tracking fixation density, heart rate variability, and pre/immediate/delayed post-tests analyzed via t-tests, ANOVA, and structural equation modeling.
result: The adaptive VR group showed higher mean knowledge gains (38.4 vs 31.2 vs 10.7), superior one-month retention (p < 0.001), elevated engagement, and immersion mediating knowledge acquisition (coefficient 0.63).
conclusion: The findings support an evidence-based framework for deploying AI-adaptive immersive learning environments in resource-varied STEM education contexts.

title: Data4Cyber: Labeled Cyber-Physical Datasets For Distribution-Grid Management Systems Under Representative Ot Attacks
authors: \"omer Sen, Lennart Bader, Marawan Emara, Martin Serror, Benedikt Schwalm, Junichi Tsurumi, Tatsumi Oba, Tomohiro Izawa, Yoshihiro Ujiie
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cyberattacks against power systems increasingly exploit industrial communication and control dependencies arising from distributed energy resources (DER), remote management, and market-based incentives. Progress on intrusion detection is constrained by a lack of public datasets that align operational technology (OT) network telemetry with physical measurements and control context. Data4Cyber is a labeled cyber-physical dataset recorded in a laboratory distribution management system (DMS) for self-consumption optimization with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, controllable loads, and substation metering. It captures synchronized process measurements, controller context, price incentives, and packet captures (Modbus/TCP and MQTT) across one benign baseline and six attack scenarios spanning protocol-semantic Modbus manipulation, man-in-the-middle (MitM) false-data injection, and MQTT price manipulation. Its fixed 1 s time base, phase-resolved labels, and state-oriented representation support temporally blocked stateful-detector evaluation. Baseline results show that high recall alone is insufficient: several detectors achieve sensitivity through alarm saturation. Context-driven attacks require process-aware interpretation rather than single-channel thresholding.
tldr: Data4Cyber is a labeled cyber-physical dataset for distribution-grid management systems under representative OT cyberattacks.
motivation: Intrusion detection research for power systems is limited by the lack of public datasets aligning OT network telemetry with physical measurements and control context.
method: The authors record synchronized process measurements, controller context, price incentives, and Modbus/TCP and MQTT packet captures in a laboratory DMS across a benign baseline and six attack scenarios.
result: Baseline detectors can achieve high recall through alarm saturation, and context-driven attacks require process-aware interpretation rather than single-channel thresholding.
conclusion: The dataset supports temporally blocked stateful-detector evaluation for cyber-physical distribution-grid security, but it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: From Attack Surface To Defense Architecture: Compositional Security For Agentic Coding Harnesses
authors: Simon Hegelich, Bardh Prenkaj, Habiba Sarhan, Morteza Shahrezaye, Kolja Hegelich, Christian Montag, Ralf Schneider, Erik Cambria
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice [MATH] and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager. Across [MATH] fixtures ([MATH] attack, [MATH] benign, [MATH] kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses [MATH] of benign work at [MATH] latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves [MATH] and [MATH] in [MATH] ([MATH] faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses [MATH] kill chains ([MATH]) and coarse Boolean taint blocks [MATH] of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves [MATH] and [MATH] at [MATH] per step.
tldr: The paper proposes ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture that secures LLM-based coding agents through capability tokens, taint lattices, and deterministic OS-level guards rather than model-level guardrails.
motivation: AI coding harnesses that give language models access to shells, filesystems, and network sockets become automated living-off-the-land platforms, and existing defenses like regex blacklists or LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails either miss structural evasions or impose high latency and over-blocking.
method: The authors introduce a Separation of Intelligence and Authority design combining Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, a 2D product taint lattice with a workspace provenance ledger, deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, bytecode certificates, and split-horizon audit logging, evaluated on attack, benign, and kill-chain fixtures with a local LLM judge baseline.
result: Ring 0 guards achieved far lower latency than the qwen3:4b LLM judge while avoiding its refusal of benign work, and in a multi-step trajectory ablation the 2D product lattice outperformed a stateless Conseca-style policy and coarse Boolean taint on kill-chain detection and benign-work retention.
conclusion: Security in agentic systems should be treated as a structural property of cognitive architecture and permission composition, and the proposed harness offers a low-latency, low-false-positive alternative to model-level guardrails.

title: Comparing WeChat And Telegram MiniApp Security Architectures: Toward Cross-Platform Analysis
authors: Luca Ferrari, Billel Habbati, Luca Verderame
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: MiniApps are increasingly central to super-app ecosystems, yet architectural differences complicate the transfer of security analysis techniques across platforms. Existing WeChat analyzers rely on packaged applications and platform-specific APIs, limiting their direct applicability to Telegram's web-based MiniApps. We present a qualitative comparison of WeChat Mini Programs and Telegram MiniApps, grounded in official documentation, prior research, and manual analysis of a specific Telegram Android source revision. Using a shared taxonomy of security controls, assets, and threat sources, we examine execution environments, communication paths, and trust boundaries. WeChat provides a dedicated MiniApp runtime; Telegram combines web execution with host controls. Both retain developer responsibilities for backend authentication and resource authorization. Two worked examples derive requirements for cross-platform analysis: distinguishing credential roles and validation boundaries, and associating host capabilities with concrete execution contexts and permission handlers. These findings inform future automated analysis without ranking the ecosystems by security or claiming validated vulnerability detection.
tldr: A qualitative comparison of WeChat Mini Programs and Telegram MiniApps security architectures aimed at enabling cross-platform security analysis.
motivation: MiniApp ecosystems are proliferating, but existing analysis tooling (e.g., WeChat analyzers) relies on platform-specific packaging and APIs, preventing direct reuse on Telegram's web-based MiniApps and motivating a shared architectural framework.
method: The authors build a shared taxonomy of security controls, assets, and threat sources, grounded in official documentation, prior research, and manual inspection of a specific Telegram Android source revision, then compare execution environments, communication paths, and trust boundaries.
result: WeChat offers a dedicated MiniApp runtime while Telegram combines web execution with host-imposed controls; both leave backend authentication and resource authorization to developers, and two worked examples derive cross-platform analysis requirements.
conclusion: The comparison informs future automated cross-platform analysis without ranking the ecosystems or claiming validated vulnerability detection.

title: What A Cage 4 Score Measures: An Audit Of A Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, And The Tables Built On Them
authors: James Rice, Ji Hwan Park, Andres Kwasinski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.
tldr: An audit of the CAGE Challenge 4 multi-agent cyber-defense benchmark showing that its scores overstate what they measure due to silent action discarding, unseeded policy sampling, and underspecified recovery-precision criteria.
motivation: Learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared on CAGE Challenge 4, but the authors suspect that reported benchmark numbers do not capture what the community assumes they do, leading to unreliable comparisons among methods.
method: The two reference defenders KEEP and H-MARL Expert are reproduced in a pinned container; the effect of the simulator's hidden busy-flag/action-discarding behavior is ablated at evaluation and in training, policy-seeding variance is decomposed, and five published comparison tables are audited for missing disclosure items.
result: Disabling the busy check costs KEEP 99.58 and H-MARL 145.98 points per episode, 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is policy sampling noise, and none of the five audited tables states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary needed for comparability.
conclusion: Benchmark scores require explicit disclosure of evaluation artifacts and seeding; the authors release the instrument, patches, traces, checkpoints and a five-item disclosure checklist to make comparisons meaningful.

title: An Empirical Study On CVE-based Vulnerabilities Propagation From One System To Another System (IntraProject Vs InterProject)
authors: Junaid Akram, Ali Hassan, Danish Vasan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerabilities in applications, including browsers, media players, online services and document readers, etc. are often exploited and cause a serious damage. The vulnerabilities could exist in your system maybe because of some coding errors, design oversights, outdated software, AI generated codes or maybe transferred from another system during development (e.g., code clones). The propagation of software vulnerabilities is a critical concern in cybersecurity. This study examines the root cause problem of vulnerabilities propagation with experiments. We analyzed the propagation of CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) based vulnerabilities within and between different software projects (IntraProject vs. InterProject). We performed several experiments on CVE based vulnerability dataset (retrieved from NVD source) by using our vulnerability detection tool (SQVDT). In the results, we discovered similar patterns of vulnerable code in several very famous recently used software, including latest version of Linux, Android operating systems, and in thousands of open source projects available on GitHub. We found several very high severity level (CVSS) vulnerabilities that propagated from one system to another system, just because of copy/paste (reuse) the code. Furthermore, we performed an empirical evaluation and verification of these vulnerable patterns that propagated to other systems by also considering the frequency of their propagation. Finlay, we recommended the impact of these vulnerabilities propagation on the interconnected systems.
tldr: An empirical study of how CVE-based software vulnerabilities propagate within and across software projects via code reuse and cloning.
motivation: Vulnerabilities often spread from one system to another through code cloning and copy-paste reuse during development, creating serious cybersecurity risks that are poorly characterized empirically.
method: The authors mine CVE vulnerability data from the NVD and analyze vulnerable code patterns within projects (IntraProject) and across projects (InterProject) using their custom detection tool SQVDT, verifying propagation frequency.
result: They find matching vulnerable code patterns in widely used software including recent Linux and Android versions and thousands of GitHub open-source projects, including high-severity CVSS vulnerabilities propagated through code reuse.
conclusion: The study documents and quantifies CVE-based vulnerability propagation across interconnected systems and recommends attention to its downstream impact on system security.

title: The Monophonic Directed Convexities
authors: J\'ulio Ara\'ujo, Ana Karolinna Maia, Thiago Marcilon, Nicolas Nisse, Rudini M. Sampaio
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph Convexity is a topic with many papers in the literature, especially on the [MATH], geodesic, and monophonic convexities in undirected graphs. Regarding directed graphs, Erd{\H o}s et al. in 1972 and Chartrand and Zhang in 2000 obtained the first results on the [MATH] and geodesic convexities for directed graphs, respectively. In this paper, we start the investigation of monophonic convexity on directed graphs. We define two convexities, the monophonic and the strong monophonic directed convexities, related to the minimal and the induced directed paths, respectively. We show that deciding whether a set is convex is polynomial-time solvable in the monophonic convexity, but coNP-complete in the strong monophonic convexity. For both convexities, we prove that the hull number is NP-complete even in DAGs. Regarding the monophonic convexity, we prove that the hull number is polynomial time solvable in tournaments, but the interval number is NP-complete in tournaments and also in bipartite oriented graphs.
tldr: This paper initiates the study of monophonic and strong monophonic convexities on directed graphs, establishing complexity results for convex set recognition, hull number, and interval number.
motivation: Graph convexity is well studied for undirected graphs (geodesic, monophonic, P3 convexities), but directed analogues have received only sporadic attention, so the authors extend monophonic convexity to the directed setting.
method: The authors define two directed convexities based on minimal directed paths and induced directed paths, then analyze the computational complexity of convex-set recognition, hull number, and interval number across graph classes such as DAGs, tournaments, and bipartite oriented graphs.
result: Recognizing convex sets is polynomial for monophonic convexity but coNP-complete for strong monophonic convexity; the hull number is NP-complete in DAGs for both, yet polynomial in tournaments for monophonic convexity, while the interval number is NP-complete in tournaments and bipartite oriented graphs.
conclusion: The work lays foundational complexity-theoretic groundwork for directed monophonic convexities and highlights sharp contrasts between the minimal-path and induced-path variants.

title: Sobolev Inequalities For The Discrete De Rham Complex And An Application To The Navier--Stokes Equations
authors: Daniele A. Di Pietro, Jerome Droniou, Marien Hanot, Silvano Pitassi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove Sobolev inequalities for the discrete de Rham (DDR) method, an arbitrary-order discretisation of the de Rham complex on polyhedral meshes. We show that, for any polyhedral domain [MATH], the DDR counterparts of the spaces [MATH], [MATH] and [MATH] satisfy the same Sobolev embeddings as their continuous counterparts. For the curl and divergence spaces, this establishes on quasi-uniform meshes an [MATH]-bound (with [MATH] in general, and [MATH] if [MATH] is convex) on discrete vector fields that are orthogonal to discrete gradients (resp.~curls), in terms of the [MATH]-norms of the vector fields themselves and their discrete curl (resp.~divergence). These Sobolev embeddings are the first such results for a polytopal complex. Their proofs hinge on recently introduced quasi-interpolators and conforming liftings. As an application, we use these estimates to prove the convergence of a DDR scheme for the Navier--Stokes equations in the curl--curl formulation. The convergence proof uses a Maxwell compactness theorem for DDR and requires no smallness assumptions on the data.
tldr: The paper proves Sobolev inequalities for the discrete de Rham complex on polyhedral meshes and applies them to convergence of a DDR scheme for the Navier--Stokes equations.
motivation: Sobolev embeddings are needed for the numerical analysis of compatible discretisations on polytopal meshes, but analogous results for discrete de Rham spaces were missing.
method: The authors establish discrete Sobolev inequalities for DDR spaces using quasi-interpolators and conforming liftings, then use these estimates together with a DDR Maxwell compactness theorem to analyse a curl--curl Navier--Stokes scheme.
result: The DDR spaces satisfy the same Sobolev embeddings as their continuous counterparts, yielding L^p bounds for curl- and divergence-orthogonal discrete vector fields on quasi-uniform meshes, and convergence of the DDR Navier--Stokes scheme without smallness assumptions.
conclusion: The work provides the first Sobolev embeddings for a polytopal complex and demonstrates their utility in proving convergence of arbitrary-order numerical schemes for fluid equations.

title: Rales: A Risk-Averse Augmented Lagrangian Equality-Constrained Sqp Method
authors: Harbir Antil, Drew P. Kouri, Denis Ridzal, Thomas M. Surowiec
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops RALES, an augmented Lagrangian method for risk-averse optimization in function spaces with nonsmooth risk measures, nonlinear equality constraints, and convex geometric constraints. The method combines safeguarded risk and constraint multiplier updates with efficient sequential quadratic programming based on inexact subproblem solves. The analysis establishes asymptotic stationarity for nonconvex problems and gives conditions for feasibility of weak primal accumulation points. Under additional assumptions on subproblem accuracy, duality, and boundedness, it provides global primal optimality guarantees and weak convergence of the full stored and candidate multiplier sequences to a common dual maximizer. Dual convergence is strong when all penalty parameters remain bounded. Numerical experiments for a finitely sampled semilinear PDE control problem, with the Conditional Value-at-Risk and the Mean-Plus-Semideviation risk measures, illustrate the method's performance as the spatial mesh is refined and as the number of samples increases.
tldr: RALES is a risk-averse augmented Lagrangian SQP method for equality-constrained optimization in function spaces with nonsmooth risk measures.
motivation: Risk-averse optimization with nonsmooth risk measures and nonlinear equality constraints in function spaces lacks efficient, provably convergent algorithms.
method: The method combines safeguarded risk and constraint multiplier updates with sequential quadratic programming using inexact subproblem solves, with asymptotic and global convergence analysis.
result: The authors prove asymptotic stationarity for nonconvex problems, feasibility of weak primal accumulation points, and global primal optimality plus dual convergence under bounded penalties; numerical PDE-control experiments with CVaR and mean-plus-semideviation illustrate performance.
conclusion: RALES provides a theoretically grounded, computationally practical framework for risk-averse PDE-constrained optimization.

title: Multiple Control Barrier Functions For Geometric Hybrid Systems: Modeling And Safe Control Synthesis
authors: Piyush P. Jirwankar, Daniel E. Ochoa, Carlos A. Montenegro G., Ricardo G. Sanfelice
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate geometric hybrid dynamical systems with states on intrinsic manifolds and inputs in topological spaces using relaxed C1-control bundles. Within this framework, we establish a barrier certificate that guarantees forward invariance of a closed set for closed-loop systems. We introduce multiple control barrier functions and derive conditions that render their sublevel sets forward invariant. We then construct pointwise optimal safe control laws, establish regularity conditions for measurable selections, and use these laws to design safety filters for geometric hybrid systems on manifolds. A second-order bouncing-pendulum example illustrates the framework and results.
tldr: The paper develops a control-barrier-function framework for safety verification and filter synthesis in geometric hybrid dynamical systems whose states evolve on manifolds.
motivation: Safety guarantees for hybrid systems with manifold-valued states and topologically constrained inputs are not well covered by existing Euclidean control barrier function theory, motivating an intrinsic geometric formulation.
method: The authors formulate geometric hybrid dynamical systems via relaxed C1-control bundles, prove a barrier certificate for forward invariance of closed sets, introduce multiple control barrier functions with sublevel-set invariance conditions, and construct pointwise optimal safe control laws with measurable-selection regularity for use as safety filters.
result: Sufficient conditions rendering sublevel sets forward invariant are derived, optimal safe controllers are characterized, and a second-order bouncing-pendulum example demonstrates the framework.
conclusion: The proposed geometric multi-barrier framework enables certified safe control synthesis and filtering for hybrid systems on manifolds, illustrated on a bouncing pendulum.

title: A Second-Order Parallel Neumann-Robin Splitting For The Stokes-Biot System With A Linear Time-Step Restriction
authors: Jeonghun Lee Yifan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we develop a second-order, fully decoupled, non-iterative partitioned method for the time-dependent Stokes--Biot problem on fixed domains. In previous work , a Robin--Robin scheme with these features was introduced, and its stability and error estimates were established under the sufficient parabolic CFL-type condition [MATH]. The main improvement of the new scheme is weakening the CFL-type condition to a linear CFL-type condition [MATH]. This can be achieved with a new splitting approach by replacing the poroelastic mechanical normal Robin condition by its physical Neumann-type traction condition, which results in a Neumann--Robin splitting. For fixed coefficients satisfying the stated assumptions, we prove a fully discrete energy bound under a restriction of [MATH]. The improvement over the parabolic restriction in the earlier Robin--Robin analysis follows from eliminating the interface residual that requires two inverse-trace estimates. We also establish an energy-norm error bound of order [MATH] under explicit regularity, finite element approximation, and initialization assumptions. Numerical experiments with manufactured solutions examine spatial and temporal accuracy and compare the Neumann--Robin and Robin--Robin schemes. A 3D cylindrical pressure-pulse benchmark further investigates their numerical stability behavior. The results distinguish the less restrictive sufficient stability condition established analytically from the observed stability thresholds of the two schemes.
tldr: The paper introduces a second-order, fully decoupled Neumann-Robin partitioned scheme for the time-dependent Stokes-Biot system, weakening the stability CFL condition from parabolic to linear.
motivation: Prior Robin-Robin partitioned schemes for Stokes-Biot required a restrictive parabolic CFL-type time-step condition, limiting practical use; this work aims to relax that restriction while preserving decoupling and second-order accuracy.
method: The authors replace the poroelastic mechanical normal Robin condition with a physical Neumann-type traction condition, yielding a Neumann-Robin splitting. They prove a fully discrete energy bound under a linear CFL-type restriction and derive an energy-norm error estimate with explicit regularity and finite element assumptions.
result: The scheme achieves a linear CFL stability restriction instead of the earlier parabolic one and obtains an energy-norm error bound. Numerical experiments with manufactured solutions and a 3D cylindrical pressure-pulse benchmark compare Neumann-Robin and Robin-Robin schemes and distinguish analytical sufficient conditions from observed stability thresholds.
conclusion: The Neumann-Robin splitting provides a less restrictive sufficient stability condition for fully decoupled partitioned Stokes-Biot simulations, though observed stability thresholds may differ from the analytical bound.

title: Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Benders Decomposition For Security-constrained Transmission Expansion Planning
authors: Jeffrey Christiansen (university Of Melbourne), Andreas T. Ernst (monash University), Terrence Mak
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy grids worldwide rely on efficient, effective and resilient transmission networks to deliver power from generators to geographically distant destinations. The optimisation problem of designing these networks is made very difficult by the non-linearity and non-convexity of the equations which govern AC power flow. In this paper we propose the Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Benders Decomposition (AMFBD) algorithm, which is capable of solving to global optimality the Security-Constrained Transmission Expansion Planning problems with N-1 redundancy, using the non-convex AC power flow equations. We demonstrate the practical capability of this algorithm by solving security-constrained expansion problems based on the Garver 6-bus problem and the 14-bus IEEE test case. Given the large costs generally associated with energy grids, globally optimal investment decisions that can be found using AMFBD have the potential to provide significant practical benefits over suboptimal solutions produced by approximations or heuristics.
tldr: The paper proposes an Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Benders Decomposition algorithm for globally optimal security-constrained AC transmission expansion planning with N-1 redundancy.
motivation: Transmission expansion planning is a difficult non-convex optimization problem due to AC power flow constraints, and practical methods often rely on approximations or heuristics that may yield suboptimal investment decisions.
method: The authors develop Adaptive Multi-Fidelity Benders Decomposition (AMFBD), a decomposition algorithm that solves Security-Constrained Transmission Expansion Planning problems to global optimality using non-convex AC power flow equations.
result: AMFBD is demonstrated on security-constrained expansion problems based on the Garver 6-bus and IEEE 14-bus test cases, showing that it can find globally optimal investment decisions.
conclusion: The proposed method offers potential practical benefits for energy grid planning by providing globally optimal solutions rather than suboptimal heuristic or approximate solutions.

title: Splitting For Stability: A Modified Reward Scheme For Transaction-Fee-Only Regimes
authors: Eric Brigham, Baigang Chen, Nicholas Hopper
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Bitcoin's block subsidy declines over time, miner revenue will come to depend increasingly on transaction fees. In fee-dominated regimes, winner-take-all reward structures can create incentives for undercutting and fork-based mining strategies, leading to instability and reduced transaction throughput. To prevent this instability, we propose a reward-splitting mechanism in which the winning block producer receives an [MATH]-portion of the block reward, while the rest is distributed among other miners; this incentivizes mining on previous blocks with higher rewards, while preserving the incentive to produce blocks with high rewards. We evaluate the proposed reward structure through analysis and simulation. Our analysis derives a local profitability condition for one-step Function-Fork deviations, showing how the winner-side reward, loser-side subsidy, and honest hash power jointly determine whether undercutting is profitable. Simulations show parameter regions in which honest behavior dominates fork-based deviations. In the cases where forking becomes dominant, the learned strategy is the least aggressive variant studied. The analysis and simulations suggest that suitable reward-splitting parameters can reduce the honest participation needed to suppress aggressive forking strategies relative to the winner-take-all structure studied in prior work. Finally, we show that the modified reward scheme does not appear to worsen selfish mining incentives. Together, these results suggest that reward redistribution can mitigate fee-driven fork incentives without introducing stronger selfish mining incentives, providing a possible direction for incentive design in fee-era proof-of-work systems.
tldr: The paper proposes a reward-splitting scheme for proof-of-work blockchains to stabilize mining incentives in transaction-fee-dominated regimes.
motivation: As Bitcoin's block subsidy declines, miner revenue becomes fee-dependent, and winner-take-all rewards can incentivize undercutting and fork-based mining that reduce stability and throughput.
method: The authors introduce a mechanism where the winning block producer receives only an α-portion of the reward while the remainder is distributed to other miners, analyzed via a local profitability condition for one-step Function-Fork deviations and validated with simulations.
result: Analysis and simulations identify parameter regions where honest mining dominates fork-based deviations, and the modified scheme appears not to worsen selfish-mining incentives.
conclusion: Reward redistribution may mitigate fee-driven forking incentives with lower honest hash power requirements than winner-take-all, offering a direction for incentive design in fee-era proof-of-work systems.

title: Early Rug Pull Detection On Solana
authors: Saba Heydaridoost, Kasra Kashani, Mohammad Mowlavi Sorond, Behnam Bahrak
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web3 platforms that help users discover and trade newly launched crypto tokens, including launchpads, decentralized-exchange (DEX) interfaces, wallets, and token-analytics sites, must assess tokens before their legitimacy is clear. On Solana, where token creation is inexpensive and tokens use standard programs rather than custom per-token smart contracts, rug pulls can unfold within minutes. Effective warnings must therefore rely on limited histories. Although graph neural networks (GNNs) have improved rug-pull detection on EVM chains, it remains unclear whether transfer structure adds predictive value over non-graph models at minute-scale decision points, and how that value changes as history accumulates. We study 2,700 tokens sampled from SolRPDS, collecting one-minute market histories from Birdeye and token transfers from Solana RPC. We define a rug pull operationally by requiring a liquidity drain, price collapse, and persistent liquidity depletion over a nominal 24-hour period after token creation. All features use only information available at or before each prediction cutoff. We evaluate observation windows of 12.5, 35.5, and 93 minutes, selected in advance from the published lifespan distribution of Solana rug pulls, and represent each token as a temporal transfer graph. Within the first 12.5 minutes, rug-pull and non-rug graphs already differ in size, density, reciprocity, and receiver-side centralization. We compare GNNs against matched non-graph models using the same token-level and graph-summary features on identical samples. A fixed panel of tokens observed in all three windows further isolates the effect of longer observation from changes in token population. Our findings inform the design of early-warning mechanisms for newly launched Solana tokens in Web3 interfaces.
tldr: This paper studies early detection of Solana token rug pulls using temporal transfer graphs and graph neural networks within minute-scale observation windows.
motivation: Web3 interfaces must warn users about newly launched tokens before legitimacy is clear, and Solana's inexpensive token creation allows rug pulls to occur within minutes, limiting available history for detection.
method: The authors analyze 2,700 tokens from SolRPDS, collect one-minute market and transfer data, define rug pulls operationally via liquidity drain and price collapse, and compare GNNs against matched non-graph models across three observation windows.
result: Rug-pull and non-rug transfer graphs differ early in size, density, reciprocity, and receiver-side centralization; the paper evaluates whether graph structure adds predictive value over non-graph features as history accumulates.
conclusion: The findings aim to inform early-warning mechanisms for newly launched Solana tokens in Web3 interfaces, but the work is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Poem: Output-Relative Block-Sparse Attention For Long-Context Prefilling
authors: Haoyi Wu, Yunkai Dang, Wanyu Zhang, Lei Wang, Wenbin Li
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.
tldr: The paper proposes TERM, an inference-time jailbreak defense for LLMs that modulates residual stream updates using prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations, avoiding any predefined safety direction.
motivation: Existing representation-based defenses rely on predefined steering directions or learned safety regions, which are hard to adapt per input and tend to cause over-refusal on benign but safety-sensitive prompts.
method: Attention entropy at each decoding step is calibrated against the prompt's own prefill baseline, then normalized and temporally accumulated to produce a bounded scaling factor applied to the model's residual updates.
result: Across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models (including Qwen3 0.6B–32B), the method is compared with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks, showing improved robustness with low over-refusal and modest inference overhead.
conclusion: Target-free, entropy-guided residual modulation offers an effective and lightweight inference-time safety mechanism for LLM deployment without requiring predefined representational targets.

title: How Well Do Sast Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using Ocpp Implementations
authors: Zachary Wadhams, Emma Sheppard, Dalton Arford, Clemente Izurieta, Ann Marie Reinhold
abstract: ArXiv:2611.14362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates globally, securing electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) software becomes increasingly critical. The Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), widely adopted for EVCS management, places significant responsibility on developers to securely implement specifications that are subject to multiple interpretations. The variety of OCPP implementations across different programming languages provides a unique opportunity to evaluate security tooling in a real-world, multi-language context where implementation variability may introduce vulnerabilities. This study provides the first empirical evaluation of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool performance across multiple programming languages using OCPP implementations as a real-world test corpus. We applied both comprehensive multi-language tools (SonarQube and Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers to twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations--each written in a distinct programming language--to examine how detection patterns vary across language ecosystems. Total issues ranged from just two in Rust to 1,689 in Java. Mature programming languages like Java yielded substantially more findings than newer languages like Rust, likely because established languages have more developed SAST tool ecosystems rather than inherently worse code quality. These results suggest that developers should consider available SAST tooling when selecting implementation languages for security critical systems.
tldr: An empirical study comparing static application security testing (SAST) tool effectiveness across twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations written in different programming languages.
motivation: EV charging infrastructure security is increasingly critical, and OCPP's specification ambiguity may lead developers to introduce vulnerabilities; the multi-language implementation landscape offers a realistic corpus for evaluating security tooling.
method: Twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations, each in a distinct language, were scanned with multi-language tools (SonarQube, Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers, and the resulting issue counts and detection patterns were compared across language ecosystems.
result: Findings varied enormously by language, from 2 issues in Rust to 1,689 in Java, with mature-language ecosystems producing more findings largely due to better-developed SAST support rather than worse code quality.
conclusion: Developers of security-critical systems should factor available SAST tooling maturity into language selection, since detection coverage is highly uneven across ecosystems.

title: Fragment-Free Constraint Programming For The Preemptive Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem
authors: M. Ang\'elica Salazar-Aguilar Vincent Boyer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.13473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This article addresses the preemptive flexible job shop scheduling problem with makespan minimization (FJm | pmtn | C_max). We propose an exact constraint programming approach that completely avoids representing the processing fragments of an operation. Operations are placed in flexible time windows, where Horn's workload condition guarantees feasible preemptive scheduling, and Jackson's preemptive earliest-deadline-first rule reconstructs exact processing segments post-optimization in O(n log n) time per machine. To manage undecided machine assignments, we extend the PreemptiveNoOverlap global constraint to optional intervals within IBM ILOG CP Optimizer, performing overload checking and preemptive edge-finding in O(n log n) time while eliminating infeasible machine alternatives. The CP model is warm-started using a multi-round MILP assignment relaxation with Carlier's head-tail bounds and a window-based greedy heuristic. Extensive computational experiments on 276 pFJSSP benchmark instances and 78 pJSSP instances demonstrate that the proposed method significantly advances the state of the art. Within a 600~s time limit, it improves the upper bounds of the previously published logic-based Benders decomposition by 3.6% on average, increases the number of proven optimal pFJSSP instances from 102 to 180, and closes 74 instances for the first time (including the entire Barnes family). On the pJSSP under identical hardware conditions, it proves 67 of 78 instances optimal (compared to 51 by the baseline solver Mistral) and closes 9 of the 11 long-standing open problems.
tldr: An exact constraint programming approach for the preemptive flexible job shop scheduling problem that avoids modeling processing fragments by using flexible time windows and reconstructing schedules with Jackson's preemptive EDF rule.
motivation: Preemptive flexible job shop scheduling (FJm | pmtn | C_max) is hard for exact solvers because fragment-based time discretization explodes the model size; the authors seek a compact exact formulation.
method: Operations are placed in flexible time windows validated by Horn's workload condition, an extended PreemptiveNoOverlap global constraint over optional intervals handles undecided machine assignments with overload checking and preemptive edge-finding in O(n log n), and the CP model is warm-started via a multi-round MILP relaxation with Carlier's head-tail bounds plus a greedy heuristic.
result: On 276 pFJSSP and 78 pJSSP benchmarks within 600 s, upper bounds improve 3.6% on average over logic-based Benders decomposition, proven-optimal pFJSSP instances rise from 102 to 180, 74 instances are closed for the first time, and 67/78 pJSSP instances (vs. 51 for Mistral) are proven optimal.
conclusion: Fragment-free constraint programming yields a substantially stronger exact method for preemptive flexible job shop scheduling, closing many long-standing open benchmark instances.
